OIL-JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Unbelievably it has been reported that the federal government will propose to the provinces tomorrow a $2 per barrel increase in the price of oil. Considering that such an increase will cause on a national basis the loss of approximately 80,000 new jobs-I say this on the basis of a study that was done by the Ontario government two years ago at the time of the last major decision for a price increase-and considering that this comes at a time when we already have more than a million unemployed in Canada, can the minister provide the House with whatever conceivable justification he can give for such an increase at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I think I have made very clear in the past the reasons for moving the Canadian price up to the international price. At present the Canadian price is the lowest price anywhere in the world. We have been criticized-and I think the hon. member has not been reluctant to add his own criticism-for our conservation measures not being what they might be. The main reason our conservation measures have been criticized by the international energy agency is that our price is so much lower than the prices in the rest of the world.
1 have also made it very clear that in addition to conservation reasons there are other reasons connected with bringing in new supplies. There is a cash flow problem and there is equally a problem with respect to the kinds of resources for which we are looking. They are a long way off and more difficult to find than they were in the past. If the hon. member is still not satisfied with that, perhaps he would like to examine the case in law and the case in politics of the producing provinces. It seems to me they have a case to make, and I am sure they will make it.

subtopic: OIL-JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The minister knows full well that other conservation measures would be more appropriate. I will preface my question. Considering that, with the present price of oil, increases of significant proportion in exploration have already taken place in Canada during the past year which would nullify the need for an increase in price to get more exploration, is the minister in agreement that this absurd proposal coming from the federal government will cost us 80,000 new jobs and, if so, what does he plan to do about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE-EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: In my view it will not have that kind of price tag at all.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, very much so. As the Minister of Finance has made clear on other occasions, and I have too, the federal government's policy is to move the price of oil toward world prices, but we have moved it rather more slowly than many have suggested we should precisely because we have tried to cushion Canadians against the increasing impact of rising prices. That in itself has been an expensive program. At present I think something like $4 billion have been provided by way of subsidies to cushion the Canadian price and at the same time to maintain a downward pressure on the price index. So we have been trying to move forward but to move in slow and measured steps.

The program objectives of the Fitness and Amateur Sport Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare are listed below in order or priority: 1. The research areas of priority in fiscal year 1976-77 and the revised listing for 1977-78 follows. These research priorities originate from external sources including national conferences, that is, National Conference on Health and Fitness, National Conference on Employee Physical Fitness, special task forces, that is, Task Force on Sport for Canadians, Sports Governing Bodies, the National Advisory Council on Fitness and Amateur Sport and others. Each research proposal submitted to its degree of relevancy to the branch's statement of research priorities for that fiscal year. If found to be sufficiently relevant, the proposal is then reviewed for significance in terms of whether the project has the potential for contributing new knowledge to the field and whether it is likely to yield findings of practical value in the solution of existing problems. A Final review is then conducted to assess the specific and technical validity of the methodology to be employed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening before ten o'clock 1 was developing the thesis that simply applying a large sum of money to improve consumer demand would not really solve the unemployment problem in this country. I indicated that there had been larger sums on the demand side this year than were included in the budget. They total some $2.4 billion. I put on the record at the end of my speech last night the unemployment figures for the two extremes, namely, Alberta and Newfoundland. I think we should look first at Alberta, the province where there is a boom in business. The unemployment rate in February for males 25 years of age and over stood at 2.9 per cent.
If one considers the largesse of the unemployment insurance funds, the number of Canadians who change addresses each year, which is 700,000, and a series of other factors which relate to the lifestyle of people in this country, one finds that 2.9 per cent is probably below the zero point in terms of actual unemployment. Probably 3 per cent to 3.5 per cent might be taken as the zero point when one considers these factors. Looking at the province of Alberta, we see in the age group 15 to 24 inclusive a rate of 9.1 per cent, a little over three times the rate for males over 25. I suggest that given another set of factors which deal with the lifestyle of young people today, and even the lifestyle of young people in my day, there would always be a substantially higher number of unemployed among this group at any given time than there would be among the male group in the age bracket from 25 up. So one can see that there is very little basic unemployment in Alberta among this age group, perhaps two or three percentage points in all.
Let us look at the other extreme, the province of Newfoundland. There we see, in contrast to 2.9 per cent for males over 25, an unemployment rate of 12 per cent, or a factor of over four. For the group of young people 15 to 24 years old, inclusive, we see 28 per cent, a factor of 2.3. We can go on for the average rates in these provinces. The average rate of unemployed of all ages in Alberta is 4.6 per cent, and the average in Newfoundland is 17 per cent. Again, this is a factor of three to four.
April 5, 1977

The point I want to make is that given these extremes, and given some other extremes that are close to them-I am thinking of the Gaspe and of all the Atlantic provinces, of northeastern Ontario, and so on-I do not think that an infusion of another $2 billion on the consumer demand side would have much effect on these situations. These are structural situations. There is a particularly bad situation in the Atlantic area. We have a bad situation among young people in many parts of the country, but particularly in the Atlantic area.
I want to deal with some suggested solutions later in my speech, but at this point the thesis I want to develop is that the problem is complex, that it is structural, and that it will not be solved by taking simple means such as the broad stroke of infusing $2 billion or $3 billion into the economy. That will not appreciably solve the problem in the Atlantic provinces. 1 reject, in particular, the simplistic claims of the NDP that we should inject more money, which was the basic thrust of their argument. 1 hope that more thought will be given to the structural nature of this problem and specifically to its regional nature with corresponding solutions.
The other point that the NDP makes in many forms is that we should be processing more of our own raw materials, something with which all Canadians would agree. Yet the NDP strongly objects to the notion that we should put more money into business and especially manufacturing or processing our raw materials. They object to allowing the business community more tax concessions, yet business investment is probably the softest spot in our whole economy. In 1973 business investment increased by 14.8 per cent, in 1974 by 7.7 per cent, in 1975 by only 5 per cent, and last year business investment actually declined by 2.9 per cent. Funds have to be made available for investment in the kind of activity the leader of the New Democratic Party talks about.
The opposition of the Tory party is a little more difficult to pin down; it is somewhat harder to define. Perhaps it is not as simplistic. There is certainly a good deal of support for many of the measures taken to further the business community. These measures amount to a little over $1.1 billion, as 1 understand it, and let us not forget that we still have the $2.4 billion going to the demand side. There was some support from the Tories for stimulating consumer demand, and 1 think there has been substantial improvement in that picture, but there seems to be the view that one way or another all this has to be done and yet the government has to cut back its budget.
All the problems we have today are a result of the government spending too much money, according to the Tories. Flow can we do all the things we are asked to do, and at the same time cut back? We did some cutting back, although not as much as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) indicated we should. He suggested we should cut back $1 billion. We cut back in the area of $650 million. 1 suppose what is bothering me about the Tory approach is their concern about our competitive position with the United States. That is
The Budget-Mr. McRae
a legitimate concern, but the Tories seem to insist that at this time, or a short time from now, controls should be removed and that that will in some way improve our competitive position. In this regard I think the Tory party and the NDP find themselves in the same camp.
I would like to discuss controls and to look at what has happened in terms of comparative cost positions. I would like to discuss our competitiveness, specifically in terms of unit labour costs. On the average per year between 1964 and 1974, Canadian unit labour costs rose 3.6 per cent, and over the same period in the United States they rose 2.7 per cent. In 1974-75, in Canada, there was a 13.8 per cent rise, and in the United States the increase was 12.1 per cent. In 1975-76, in Canada, unit labour costs rose 9 per cent in Canada and 4 per cent in the United States. In 1976-77, Canadian unit labour costs rose 7.5 per cent, and in the United States they rose 5 per cent. In Canada, unit labour costs have risen steadily, but they have consistently risen faster than they have in the United States. This has created some very serious problems for our government and our economy.
I feel that the controls should stay for some period of time. On the price side, in 1975 Canada was seventh on the list of 24 OECD countries, and by the fall of 1976 we were in fourth position in terms of reducing or keeping prices down. The countries which were ahead of us were Switzerland, which was number one, Germany, which was number two, and the United States, which was third. That was in October of 1976, and those are the latest figures I have.
Labour's share of net income will give us an idea of what gains have been made. In 1975, labour's share of our net income was 73 per cent. In 1976, it rose to 74.3 per cent. The profits of corporations initially took 14.8 per cent of our net income, but that figure decreased to 13 per cent. 1 think there is some justification for our concern about the business community, and in terms of labour getting its share I think we should keep the controls.
I would like to wrap up my remarks by indicating that I am concerned because the debate in this House has been of a simplistic nature. We are not looking carefully enough at the ingredients which make up our economy; we are not analysing them. In the two or three minutes which are left, I would like to make some suggestions. I feel an effort was begun in this budget-and I think we have to extend that effort-to regionalize the federal government. I was very pleased by the relatively small-but significant in terms of our future- change in fiscal policy. We have said that the 5 per cent investment tax credit will be extended to the whole country, but that in areas of northern Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan it will rise to 7.5 per cent, and in the Atlantic provinces, where problems really exist, this credit will rise to 10 per cent. That is a beginning. I believe it is a first. It certainly is a first as far as my memory is concerned. It is the very beginning of a fiscal policy which has a regional base. It is an extremely important start. I think that following up that start cannot be left just to DREE. DREE is doing a Fine job, but it cannot do the job alone.

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Clark
I think our efforts must be multidepartmental. I suggest that perhaps there should be more fiscal measures. I suggest that perhaps more should be put into direct job creation. Our transportation system is very much involved in our development.
Mr. Speaker, 1 just need one more minute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suggest that transportation will play an important role in developing our regions. There are many other departments which could become involved. For instance, some months back we were talking about the "Orion." About $500 million worth of work was to be created in Canada, but at that time nobody thought about creating that work outside the centres of the two cities involved, and creating it in regions where problems exist. In everything we do we should be conscious of the fact that these regions, which might be called undernourished, must be taken care of.
I suggest that we might also look at the possibility of separate monetary policies for some of these regions. This is very tricky and is something that one has to look at carefully, but it is a possibility. 1 am suggesting over-all that we not turn the country back to the provinces but, rather, that we learn how to develop regional economies under the federal system.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to state that I hope the debate will deal more basically with the problems rather than taking the broad stroke; that there will be more imagination, particularly when we are thinking of regionalization, and that there will be a kind of getting away from the "we", "they" position that we have where "we" on the labour side say "they" should not have it, or "we" on the corporate side say "they"-labour-should not have it. At this crucial point, when problems are so interdependent and so complex, there is a much greater need for understanding among all sectors of Canadian society.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday night, in the budget speech, the government missed its last chance. We now know that this government is unable to provide the country with the leadership it needs and that it rallies politicians who can give stage performances in Washington but cannot govern Canada. Even at this late stage, the budget could have met three objectives. It could have created jobs for the thousands of Canadians who are looking for one, particularly among young people and in the eastern provinces.
It could have put money into the pockets of low-income Canadians to lighten their tax burden and stimulate the demand for Canadian products. Finally it could have restored an atmosphere of confidence in the Canadian economy, par-

ticularly among investors. But since last Thursday night, we are even a little farther from those objectives. The opportunity went by. Nobody grabbed it.

Mr. Speaker, this government opposite, which has been running the affairs of this nation for the last nine years, has very much to answer for. Its most dramatic failure has been its failure to bring Canadians together-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -its failure to unite Canada. This government came to office in the year of Expo, the year of centennial when the spirit of unity in this country was never higher. Now, it has never been lower after nine years of the government's administration. At least in this area of attempting to unite the country the government had an approach; it had a policy; it seemed to know what it wanted to do, but in the area of economics there has been no pattern, no policy, no consistent objectives.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No leadership.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There have been no results except the results that are felt by the more than one million Canadians who are out of work now. In making policy, we have endured under this government a decade of drift. There was an opportunity for the minister to change that and to bring some direction to economic policy in this country on budget night last week. The government refused absolutely to respond to the challenge of bringing leadership to Canada.
Mr. Speaker, one of the most outstanding features of this government is the energy it devotes to spreading the blame to others and fixing on others blame for its own failures.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is always somebody else.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is always somebody else, as one of my colleagues says. This budget is very much in the tradition of blame-fixing; it is a blame-fixing budget; it is an attempt to find scapegoats. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) attributes the decline in activity in equity investment markets to "such unsettling factors as the world recession, oil price increases, inflation and poor corporate earnings." When we look for unsettling factors, we need look no further than across the floor of this House of Commons.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The main unsettling factor in the economy of Canada is this indecisive, drifting, insensitive government itself. Again, sir, the minister attributes the unemployment situation in Canada to "rapid growth and changes in the structure" of the Canadian labour force, as if this were a sudden volcanic eruption unforeseeable by mere mortals, yet both the increase of young people seeking jobs and the increase of women seeking jobs has been forecast for years by the government's own statisticians. The arrival of a new generation of jobless-the Big Mac generation-has been known and expected for at least 15 years, and in each and every year of
April 5, 1977

the last decade the participation rate of adult women in the labour force has trended upward by a predictable, foreseeable 1 per cent per year. The situation has been foreseeable for anyone who cared to look-indeed, for anyone who cared at all about Canada. Yet the plain fact is-as illustrated again by the budget brought down last Thursday night-that this government does not care about anything except about its own month to month survival. I simply say that the new attempt to fix the blame somewhere else is not going to work this time because the day is coming when the people of Canada will put the blame for political disunity and economic stagnation right where it belongs-squarely at the top, with the political leadership of this nation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), who is out of the House for the time being, has outside this House called this budget a Tory budget. Sir, would that it were. 1 wish that the socialist leader was, on this occasion, and for once, in touch with reality. In fact, if the parentage of this budget lies anywhere other than with this government, it rests with the New Democratic Party and with those heady days from 1972 to 1974-those days when the NDP came as close to power as they ever will; those days when this government was so ready to mortgage the country's future to buy the support of the NDP.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If this were a Tory budget, as the leader of the New Democratic Party suggests, it would be a far more effective document than the one brought down last Thursday night.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), indicated yesterday, it would have included real and generous tax cuts for lower income earners, not just the scraps from Big Mac's table.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame on you, Mac.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would have included selected reductions in the manufacturers' sales tax as a measure to reduce the cost of living for ordinary Canadians. It would have included stronger steps in support of small business.
Today we saw the minister responsible for small business standing up and boasting about the high rate of failure of businesses under the Liberal administration. Their advice to students seeking jobs is to leave the country. Their advice to small businessmen is, if they stay in the country under a Liberal government, they can be sure to fail. Sir, a Conserva-
The Budget-Mr. Clark
tive budget would have included, in order to bring jobs and investment to the disadvantaged regions of Canada, stronger measures such as long-term tax contracts for firms prepared to invest in those regions.
These are all positions which my colleagues and I have been outlining in this House and elsewhere in the country, hoping that the Minister of Finance would take cognizance of the proposals we have offered and of the seriousness with which this country regards the economic stagnation which is the legacy of the decade of drift under the present Liberal government.
Above all, a budget prepared by our party would have restored a sense of confidence, direction and purpose to the economy of Canada. It is of some note that this government has finally seen the need to encourage new investment in Canada, has finally seen the linkage between investment, jobs and growth. But what has been gained on that side has been more than lost, again, by the minister's continuing confusion about controls. The minister asserts baldly that the controls program "has helped to bring down the rate of inflation." Yet there is little evidence for that assertion. It is true that the rate of increase in consumer prices in Canada is less than it once was. But it is also true that in most parts of the industrialized world it is less than it once was. In fact, consumer prices are still rising faster in Canada, with controls, than they are in the United States without controls.
Sir, to accept without criticism the minister's assertions about the role of controls is to commit a primitive, logical fallacy. We can expect primitive actions from this government, but one might think that it would be good at arid logic. The line of the minister, in effect, is that rain follows the rain-dance; one causes the other. The minister, who is all too ready to believe in mysterious outside forces when it suits him-for example, when it comes to unemployment-would have us forget altogether about outside forces when it comes to assessing the value of his economic program, particularly the program of controls. The truth is that the main value of controls lies in the time they can buy the government in order to put into place real and lasting solutions. That is the essence of the matter which the government still does not understand. That was the essence of the economic stabilization program proposed by this party and attacked so vigorously by the government opposite in the 1974 election campaign.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
