subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, they are devising another budget.

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Clark

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Even though the main purpose of a controls program is to buy time with which to put other reforms into place, this government has wasted that one asset, wasted those precious 18 months of time. Indeed, this government specializes in waste. It wastes the people's assets. It wastes the people's money. It wastes the people's time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It wastes people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And it wastes people, as my colleague says. When controls were introduced we were promised a comprehensive energy policy for Canada, yet 17 months later we still have no comprehensive energy policy for Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not even have a comprehensive promise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague said we do not have a comprehensive promise. Seventeen months ago we were promised a housing policy. Today there is no co-ordinated housing policy. Seventeen months ago we were promised that the government would examine the impact of regulatory practices on economic performance and efficiency. Yet we have seen no evidence at all that such an examination has been carried out. The government has wasted the time it bought.
As 1 have said on previous occasions, what Canadians demanded above all else from this budget was a sense of reassurance. They needed some sense of certainty on which they could make plans and from which they could draw some sense of confidence. They wanted to be told where this government was heading in terms of its basic economic policy so that individual Canadians, the decision-makers across this country who make this economy tick, could decide where to head with some sense of certainty and assurance.
Instead, on the central issue of the current controls regime, this minister's performance was nothing short of ludicrous. He started out by saying flatly that the job of controls was "not yet done"-and, indeed, his budget document restated the expiry date of December 31, 1978. But then he told us that there was-and I quote him-"a particular need to consider a possible date for beginning the decontrol process." There we had something specific. He mentioned the need to consider a possible date for beginning. And what is that date, Mr. Speaker? Well, the minister is not quite sure. He said, again, and 1 quote him, that it would be "neither feasible or desirable" to begin that process before October 14. But wait a minute. There is this question of voluntary restraint. If there is any progress there-and the minister does not bother to tell us or the other partners in the economy what he regards as progress-it may be that he will consider an earlier date. But he is telling everyone to proceed, as he puts it, "in the expectation that controls will continue in effect for some time." So we have a government that is on every side of the question as to when, whether, or how controls will terminate.
Instead of that confusion, this country needed certainty and reassurance. But what we got from the minister was confusion and mumbo-jumbo. Compared with that performance, Mr. King's famous phrase about conscription is clear and unequivocal.
[Mr. Epp.J
The tragedy, sir, is not how foolish this minister and this government look. We and the country are well used to the government and the minister looking foolish. The tragedy is that by refusing to give Canadians any clear sense of direction on this essential question, the minister probably has undone any stimulative effect he might have obtained from the various investment incentives he offered in his budget. With one hand he offers Canadians tax benefits for new investment and expansion in the economy, but with the other he maintains and even increases the very climate of uncertainty which has already done so much damage to our prospects and potential for growth. This government, to borrow a phrase, already has wrestled investment to the ground. The minister on Thursday night simply threw it for another fall.
Sir, the budget calls for a deficit of almost $7 billion. It is, as my colleague for York-Simcoe said yesterday, a deficit larger than the entire federal budget when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) led the government of Canada. It is a deficit which adds almost $800 to the burden of national debt carried by every working Canadian.
Yet, sir, not only is it a large deficit; it is a do-nothing deficit. It adds flab, not muscle, to our economy. It is not the result of any conscious government decision to stimulate the economy and put people to work. Deficits can be justified if they create jobs, but the only jobs this deficit will provide are for the people who operate the printing presses for the Bank of Canada.
What this deficit represents is this year's cost to Canadians of the past extravagance and the continuing irresponsibility of the government. What it shows us with such frightening clarity is the extent to which this government's wild spending habits during the past nine years have come home to roost. This government has so overextended itself and so overextended the resources of Canadians that even when it stands still its accounts fall deeper into the hole. In short, this budget deficit has nothing to do with the economic theories of John Maynard Keynes. It has everything to do with the economic irresponsibility of John Napier Turner.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Given the minister's debt to his predecessors, it is useful to observe that neither of his two predecessors chose, after serving in the finance portfolio, to seek re-election to the House of Commons. The electors of Kingston and the Islands, and the electors of Ottawa-Carleton, now are represented by Progressive Conservatives. We have to ask if the electors of Rosedale can be far behind.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A budget prepared by this party would, as I say, have restored a sense of confidence and direction to the Canadian economy, not merely because there are better ideas on this side of the House-and that is obvious-but because we in this party know the basic economic goals that we would
April 5, 1977

set for Canada. Our government would reaffirm unequivocally that it is the private sector which is the main source of new jobs and new wealth in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Elear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Our government would recognize its responsibility to establish a climate of certainty so that the private sector could get on with the job of building the country. Government has a right and a responsibility to establish the rules within which the economy operates, but it has an obligation, also, to ensure that those rules are fair and precise and that they are not subject to change in the middle of the night, as has been the case too often with this government.
Our government would establish a tax system which encourages Canadians to channel their savings, now among the world's highest on a per capita basis, toward new investment in this country. Our government would give the private sector room to grow by reducing its own demands upon our productive citizens.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe, pointed out yesterday, 20 cents of every dollar earned by Canadians is claimed by personal income taxes, compared with just 14 cents in the United States. A Conservative government would be committed to reducing that load on the individual Canadian taxpayer. Finally, our government would take the lead in strengthening Canada's competitive position in the world, not merely as a passing, budgetary gimmick but in the long-term interests of this nation.
I want to speak for a moment about the grim statistics of unemployment in this country. I suppose the budget was merely an elaboration of the definitive statement of government policy on unemployment that was offered to students at the University of Toronto the other day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he said, "If you want a job, leave this country."

The problem of unemployment is particularly acute in the province of Quebec and in the four Atlantic provinces. Last February, Quebec alone accounted for almost a third of the total number of unemployed. It is obvious that those men and women found no comfort in that budget and certainly no hope. But unemployment is not just a statistical issue, it is a social problem resulting in all kinds of human tragedies. Unlike the government members, we are very concerned by this problem.
The general impression given by this government is this: we have no reason to be overly concerned about unemployment because the unemployed can claim unemployment insurance or, at worst, live on welfare. Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely against such an attitude as it is completely indefensible. Such a cynical and pessimistic position does not have its place in Canadian society. Such a reasoning ignores a basic value, that of human dignity. It also forces upon society a cost in human monetary resources that it is not supposed to assume. Further-
The Budget-Mr. Clark
more, it is surely not on such a basis that we shall build our country and achieve all its potential.

It is essential, if we are going to build in this country and if we are going to realize the potential we possess, that we create among the new generation of Canadians, the young who are now coming into the work force and looking for work, some sense, not just of the greatness of this country but of the possibility for each of them to find some way in which he or she can contribute to the building of this country.
We hear a lot of talk these days about the attitudes of our young people. Some question their commitment to the work ethic, although, as I have said before, the work ethic requires having some work to be ethical about. The Prime Minister questions the expectations of the young. He suggests that young Canadians have no right to believe that Canada owes them a job opportunity and a future. Others worry about the cynicism of the young, especially their lack of respect for and belief in our political institutions.
I invite hon. members to look at this budget from the point of view of a young Canadian, and ask themselves what this budget and what this government offers a young Canadian other than cynicism and disbelief. This is a budget that tells young Canadians baldly, without apology or compassion, that this government is not prepared to deal with unemployment. If that were not enough, it is a budget which adds several more billion dollars to the legacy of waste and extravagance for which the next generation ultimately will have to pay.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With a government like this and a budget like that produced on Thursday night, it is no wonder that we have a generation which is being schooled in cynicism and hopelessness? This dismal budget begs any number of questions, but no question is more fundamental than the simple one: Why, given the very real problems facing the Canadian economy, would the minister choose to give us a budget that addresses none of these problems? Why, given the current need for some sense of certainty and reassurance, would the minister offer the country only new confusion and new uncertainty? Perhaps the most direct and, indeed, kindest explanation is that this government is simply too incompetent to deal with the country's problems. There is no lack of evidence that this government has long since run out of any steam that it ever had.
Another possible explanation is that this government in fact has a very limited view of what this country can achieve, a very limited view of the possibilities of Canada. It does not seek to achieve our growth potential as a country because it does not really think we have any. It really is not seized with the problem of one million unemployed Canadians-with more coming, thanks to this budget-because it accepts unemployment as a norm for Canada. Besides, do we not have a generous unemployment insurance program in this country? This kind of reasoning can cause us to lose forever the chance

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
to achieve the potential of this country. If that, indeed, is the view of this government-and there are plenty of musings from the Prime Minister to suggest that it is-then, bluntly, this government is simply not worthy of this country. This country, with all its potential, deserves much more than a government whose highest ambition is to stand still. The people of Canada deserve better than a government which sees the Canadian dream as being two parts unemployment insurance and one part welfare.
There is a third possible explanation for this budget, Mr. Speaker, one so cynical that I would not attribute it to any government but this one. It is that the minister's budget decisions were made on the basis, not of Canada's economic needs but of the Liberal party's electoral strategy. If there is to be no election in 1977, then why waste any effective action this yeaf? Next year is when the government needs the "goodies". So one million Canadians will just have to wait until Keith Davey gives them the green light.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I would not even suggest such a cynical approach by any government other than this one. But I look back at this government's economic policies and I ask myself whether they have ever had any basis other than sheer political opportunism. In 1968, in that famous election campaign, the Prime Minister went around the country-this should be remembered in light of his record-telling Canadians that it was time to "end the free stuff'. That from the right hon. member for Mount Royal! Then he went on the wildest spending binge in Canadian history.
In 1974 the Liberal campaign strategy-their "promise for tomorrow"-was to point out of television sets at Canadians and say, "Zap, you're frozen", and then to introduce the very controls regime that they had attacked. Canadians, looking at that record, will ask themselves whether this government is not capable of putting aside the needs of Canada if they do not happen to fit in with the plans of the Liberal party. I will let this House and the country decide which of those explanations best fits this unworthy government. Canadians can decide whether this government is simply incompetent, whether it has no faith in Canada, or whether it is just too cynical to care. Canadians can make that choice, Mr. Speaker, for these questions all lead to the same conclusion. There is simply no justification for this government to remain in office, and the sooner Canadians get their right to change that, then the better for all of us.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lessard (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you ready to resign?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member across the way asks if I am ready to resign. He will probably have to wait a good long while for me to do that. Chances are I shall be here in the House for a long time to come while he probably will not.
Mr. Speaker, I listened very closely to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I was hoping that, after

leading his party for a year, he would have fare more interesting solutions to suggest than those we heard. Of all he said, which I followed closely, I found it hard to remember more than three or four points that may have some value, which could possibly be analysed had he given us more details. But, as always, the Leader of the Opposition abstained from giving us details of what his party could really offer. He limited himself to great general statements.
For the so-called disadvantaged areas of the country, he said, he would have a huge program of decentralization and he of course would resort to incentive measures to help investments in those areas. It is all very well, Mr. Speaker, to make such statements; it is a very easy solution. We do that too, we have done so. We often hear, publicly, men who are not necessarily active in politics, make such statements. But there is a huge difference between declarations of principle and concrete action, and detailed proposals; there is a huge difference, because it is always more difficult when time comes to do exactly what one has said one would do. I should like to point out to the Leader of the Opposition that, last fall, when he spoke to students in the Maritimes, and in New Brunswick in particular, he dared say that one of the prime concerns of a Progressive Conservative government with regard to the Atlantic provinces would be to decentralize the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
He did not even know then that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion had already been decentralized for more than two years. He said in one of his last comments that a Tory government would promote the investment of the large savings made by the Canadian people. Indeed he insisted on the fact that those savings were highest among industrialized countries. Why, Mr. Speaker, do Canadians have such large savings? It is precisely because the government during the past few years has taken steps to encourage Canadians to save and invest in the development of their country. The budget tabled last Thursday by my colleague suggests other formulas to encourage Canadians to invest more of their savings in the development of industry.
Mr. Speaker, I am quite pleased to take part this afternoon in the debate on the budget speech. I am proud to do so as a Canadian and a Quebecer from the Lac-Saint-Jean area. Any thorough consideration of the Canadian economic conditions and prospects brings us to the conclusion that the success has been mitigated and that the future is uncertain if the present trends are maintained. The budget put forward last Thursday by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) clearly indicates the way to a greater prosperity. The Canadian economy has the following challenge to offer: as citizens we should rely more on our own resources than on the government to improve our individual conditions. By doing otherwise we would lead the existing welfare programs to bankruptcy. As workers, we should expect long term wage increases only when we can increase our productivity. By doing otherwise, Mr. Speaker, we would force companies to close down and we would lose our jobs.
April 5, 1977

As managers, Mr. Speaker, we should reinvest more money in our business and become more competitive internationally through better decisions and a more efficient marketing policy for our products. As groups of manufacturers, Mr. Speaker, we should limit our dependence on tariffs which are too often used only to conceal our lack of innovation, and we should increase our efforts in research and development.
Mr. Speaker by doing otherwise, we would impair our conviction that free enterprise prevails in our economy. As a government, we should account each year for our programs both as far as their efficiency and as their implementation are concerned. By doing otherwise, we would keep implementing obsolete programs and provide inadequate services.

The government remains convinced that the proper longterm policy for economic growth in this country is to regain our competitive position internationally by ensuring that inflation is controlled and increased productivity is encouraged. This will lead to more jobs and more exports. This will lead to an increased capital investment. At the same time, the federal government is committed to continuing restraint in its own growth and spending policies. By controlling its own spending, the federal government sets an example to the other levels of government that they, too, should control their growth instead of depending on increased transfer payments from Ottawa.
By limiting our spending policies we are leading Canadians to the conclusion that in the final analysis the country relies on them and their efforts. To get the economy moving again we will have to bring high inflation and its accompanying psychology under strict control. We can, then, bring wage settlements in line and control our unit labour costs, thus improving our international competitive rating position. As productivity increases, the real income of Canadians will rise accordingly. Private sector decisions to invest will lead to less government spending and decreasing demands on social programs.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to say that the federal government's budget takes into consideration the problems mentioned and the alternatives proposed and brings forward appropriate solutions.
My colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), stated, and 1 quote:
Our first objective must be to maintain the underlying trend to lower inflation.
Our second objective must be to encourage a steady and non-infiationary growth in the economy, in order to provide jobs and reduce unemployment.
I want to emphasize that the federal government recognizes and accepts its responsibility for action to help achieve these goals. But responsibility for the economy rests on others as well. Both political and economic power are widely dispersed in this country, reflecting Canada's diversities and protecting our fundamental liberties. All those who share power also share the responsibility that goes with it for the attainment of our economic goals.
Mr. Speaker, the measures proposed in the budget speech will certainly create employment, foster investments and favour regional development. They will improve the stock market as well as the liquid assets of companies, thereby
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
making funds available for expansion. They will also provide increased assistance to small and medium size business.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear! That is what a real government is, Marcel, a real one-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Moreover, let us consider for a moment the direct creation of employment in certain areas where unemployment is very high; let us think of the incentives to increase investments, including the self-financing of firms to compensate for the stagnation of benefits and the distortions resulting from inflation; let us think of the encouragements to small business, the lightening of the burden of the Canadian taxpayer, especially those whose revenues are affected most by inflation. There is, however, in the budget speech an item which interests me in the highest degree, Mr. Speaker, namely the extension for an additional three years, that is, up to July 1, 1980, of the investment tax credit program.
As a complement, its rate is increased to lxh per cent for the areas designated by our department, that is Saskatchewan, Manitoba, northern Ontario and Quebec, except for the Mont-real-Hull corridor and the Gaspe peninsula. For the Gaspe peninsula and the Atlantic provinces, the rate has been increased to 10 per cent. That means that a company located in the Atlantic area will be able to deduct from its federal income tax the equivalent of 10 per cent of its new investment. Thus, a company with $100,000 investment could deduct $5,000 before. Now it will be able to deduct $10,000.
Money is important, but it will never be as important as the concept itself. For the First time, a fiscal tool will be used to fight against regional disparities. This is a first step and cause for rejoicing. Why should it not be the same with personal income tax? Why should it not be the same with other measures likely to convince people, for example, to remain in the Atlantic area?
And I would even go further, Mr. Speaker, why would it not be possible to help Canadians who were born in the Atlantic provinces, who were educated there and who, because of a lack of jobs, moved to central Canada where they took up a career in business, industry or other fields? Why not provide an incentive to allow those people who in many cases retire before time, that is before they are 65, to go back to their region and give the local small businesses and people the benefits of their business experience in central Canada?
I think, Mr. Speaker, we could find some formula that would prompt these citizens to go back to their native areas and make their experience benefit their younger fellow-citizens and organisations. That is a suggestion 1 am now making. This is the first time I do so publicly and I am quite prepared, now that the Minister of Finance has already listened to me, to continue pressuring him so he will again listen to the recommendations I might put forward on other occasions.
As 1 was saying, Mr. Speaker, it is the first time that the Canadian tax system recognizes there are differences between the various parts of the country. The new tax credit providing for three various rates is to give an additional incentive to investment in those areas where the economic recovery is the

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
slowest and the unemployment rate the highest. The tax credit applicable to other areas of Canada remains at 5 per cent. This 5 per cent tax credit was set up in 1975 and turned out to be, as my colleague the Minister of Finance pointed out, a significant incentive for our manufacturing and processing industries. I would like to commend him for extending it for another three years and applying different rates in various regions. It is something which will be quite welcome by isolated areas.
Of course, as evidenced by its creation, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion had long recognized the existence of those disparities. It recognized them when it applied its politics because consideration is being given to those regional differences in our policy, for instance in the agreements we are currently negotiating and concluding with the provincial governments. Cost-sharing arrangements resulting from their application vary from one province to another. Those arrangements go from a 50-50 per cent basis in some provinces such as Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia to a 40 per cent provincial and 60 per cent federal in provinces such as Quebec, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. And in the case of the Atlantic provinces, as far as 90 per cent of the expenses incurred are paid by the federal government. That is a genuine and factual recognition, Mr. Speaker, and not mere words, not promises but precise facts which can be verified every day.
As member for Lac-Saint-Jean and minister of the Crown- and as Minister of Regional Economic Expansion-and in the name of my department, I undertake personally to take up the challenge contained in the budget and follow up its objectives through our programs and initiatives.
In my estimation, my Department of Regional Economic Expansion is perhaps the one federal department best suited for the implementation of the budget's philosophies of employment creation, business investment incentives and development of regional growth.
In the past three years, since the beginning of the general development agreement mechanism between my department and the provincial governments, nearly 70 subsidiary agreements have been signed, more than 20 of them in the fiscal year just ended. Several of these new agreements were co-signed with me by the federal Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand). These action pacts raise to well over $2 billion the total committed to regional development initiatives through these subagreements, including an industrial park in Wabush, Newfoundland; community infrastructures in Happy Valley, Goose Bay, Labrador; agricultural development in Nova Scotia; an examination of potential major coal development in British Columbia; and land and air transportation improvements in northern Alberta, to name but a few.
With even this briefest of summaries, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that DREE's scope for correcting regional disparities is national and that we are effective both in direct industrial
development and in joint consultation and program development between the federal and the provincial governments. In everything we do, we actively foster regional growth. We support small business creation and expansion. We assist farmers and fishermen and foresters. In conjunction with provincial governments we plan rural development strategies and we have a direct effect on regional industrial development strategies. At all stages we are generating new employment opportunities and ensuring decent job alternatives to citizens in rural or slow-growth areas.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the business incentive program. As we all know, the Regional Development Incentives Act has now become a well established program. Companies from all parts of Canada have received grants which amount to more than $580 million. This should lead to some 127,500 new jobs in slow growth areas.
I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the success rate of companies which have received grants is about 90 per cent. Furthermore the application of this program has been constantly improved to meet the requirements of industry. For example, the delay required for analyzing applications for grants has been reduced by 25 per cent since 1974. When the decision is taken at the regional level, which is the case for more than 80 per cent of the applications received by the department, the delay required to consider the application and to come to a decision has been reduced by 33 per cent. [English]
All across Canada the year ahead promises to be difficult and exacting, politically and economically. 1 pledge my department to continued consultation with every provincial government to identify and resolve regional problems.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In keeping with our effort to bring government services closer to the people who use them, I will soon be announcing new offices in regional centres to service development needs. To meet inordinately high unemployment levels in major industrial centres I will pursue new concepts in priority industrial development programs. I and my department will continue to extend our programs and services to the status and non-status native people in co-operation with the provincial governments.
In British Columbia the central economic problem is the province's reliance on a single resource-based industry. When, as now, that industry suffers in a world market slump, the whole province suffers. My department is currently involved, along with other federal departments and the provincial government, in a thorough examination of industrial development alternatives for British Columbia, both in primary resources and in secondary manufacturing. We hope to help create long-term jobs in British Columbia that will not be threatened by slack world markets in any single industry.
In the prairie provinces the central problems facing Canadians are a potentially severe water shortage and a chronic lack

April 5, 1977

of a mature industrial base. My department, through the PFRA, will continue to develop water drainage systems and other flood control systems to better conserve water holdings. With both the subagreements and the RD1A program we will work together with the provincial governments and community groups to develop that much-needed industrial base.
In Ontario, easily the most industrialized and most populous province, serious regional disparity continues unchecked. My department will provide continuing RDIA and subagreement incentives to rural or regionally based Ontario citizens with particular focus on the rural and small town communities in eastern Ontario. In the Atlantic provinces the challenge is twofold. We must strive to narrow the gap between the region and the more affluent central core, and at the same time give high priority to closing the gap between the metropolitan areas and the more rural areas within the Atlantic region. Under the special areas programs the metropolitan economies were greatly strengthened. In recent years DREE has increasingly shifted its priorities toward the non-urban areas. This is a trend which will continue.
Our spending in the Atlantic region more and more favours the non-urban areas, as the following figures will illustrate. Under the GDA program and the P.E.I. development plan we have committed the following to rural areas: 76 per cent of our spending in Newfoundland; 78 per cent of our spending in New Brunswick; 45 per cent of our spending in Nova Scotia- and this does not include DEVCO spending: all budget expenditures take place in one area of the province-and 92 per cent of our spending in Prince Edward Island goes to the rural part of the province.
In short, almost 75 per cent of our Atlantic commitments are in non-urban parts of the region. To be sure we will not want to endanger the economies of the Atlantic metropolitan areas. We must be, and are, however, committed as a department to close the income gap within provinces as well as between provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal briefly with the present situation in Quebec. As I said to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce last Tuesday, we intend intensifying our activity in the Montreal area while working closely with local administrations. Montreal is presently going through a difficult period. In recent months, the rate of unemployment has risen rapidly to a high of 9.2 per cent in February, while it was only 6.8 per cent in the greater Toronto area, 8.3 per cent in Halifax, 4.8 per cent in Regina and 3.5 per cent in Edmonton.
In view of the fact that almost half of unemployed Quebecers are in the greater Montreal area, that the economic development of Quebec must come out of the revitalizing of the Montreal growth rate, that the Quebec economy is handicapped by the current structural decline of Montreal, that such a decline results from a gradual weakening of the relative situation of Montreal in certain key areas such as transportation and financial activities which are traditionally at the very base of the development of that area, it is obvious that we shall have to intervene to remedy the current situation. How will the
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
government finally choose to do so? We do not know that in full details as yet, Mr. Speaker. Nevertheless, as officials of DREE, we shall go on negotiating subagreements under the General Development Agreement signed with Quebec.

In summary, I accept on my own behalf and on behalf of my department the three budgetary challenges of employment creation, investment encouragement and regional development. As Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, I will strive to achieve a better balance in Canada's economic growth so that rural or small town Canadians will not be forced, through lack of meaningful employment opportunities in their home regions, to move to already overcrowded urban areas, occasionally with high levels of unemployment. In many cases, my department will work closely together with other federal departments, provincial governments and the private sector to take advantage of regional development opportunities. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the coming year is going to be very demanding, politically and economically. And to accept the challenge of encouraging our national unity by an increased understanding of the regional problems and of the solutions which will have to be found, not one federal department is better equipped than the DREE.
The Minister of Finance said in his speech, and I quote:
with a market economy and within a federal State government, responsibility for the economy does not rest only on the federal government. It rests on all Canadians. Both political and economic power are widely dispersed in this country, reflecting Canada's diversities, and protecting our fundamental liberties. All those who share power also share the responsbility that goes with it.
I repeat this, Mr. Speaker, as it is a very important statement. It answers as well some of the critics who would consider the government as the sole body responsible for the economic problems which face the country today and confront unfortunately too many jobless Canadians.
But the responsibility does not rest only on the Canadian government. We all share these responsibilities: the provincial governments, the population at large and the private sector are all responsible for this situation, up to a certain point. This has never been so true, especially within the present political context in Canada and particularly in Quebec.
For instance, we see advertisements inviting industrialists to leave Quebec. Those people bear on their shoulders the future of our country and I hope they are conscious of what they are doing. To those people I would like to recall the frustration which people from the Atlantic area are living with or have lived with for many years, the frustration that Quebecers experience, as do all the people living in isolated areas. That could be ascribable to the carelessness of the governments, but especially to the business community which is more interested in immediate profits and much less in the general well being of the population. Industry still has to find a social conscience.
Too often business and industry forget that if Canada falls apart, their profits will also disappear and if they concentrate

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Lessard
their investments too much in the centre of the country or in large cities, they work against national unity and consequently they work against their own long term interests.
Current economic development often operates to the detriment of the Atlantic and Quebec areas and northern parts of all provinces.
I think that if industry, businessmen, really have the interest of this country at heart, if they believe that its interest is their interest, if they want this country to continue to exist and progress they will have to understand that the basic condition is that they reconsider their approach to investment. If industry separates the Canadian economy from the Quebec economy, the only thing left for Quebecers to do will be to achieve political independence, and that would be a situation that I would regret deeply. This message is fundamental and I feel strongly about it and I am glad that the budget speech deals with it.
My colleague, the Minister of Finance, said in this way the private sector also has some power and responsibility. In our market economy private business takes most investment decisions and looks for new outlets in and outside Canada in competition with one another and with foreign suppliers. The private sector basically develops the new resources and new techniques that allow us to maintain and improve the standard of living. Governments can, of course, provide assistance and incentives but experience proves that we are better off leaving those decisions to the private sector. Efforts by private business, its judgement and faith in the future are indispensable to economic progress. More then ever it is time for unity among all members of this Canadian society. It is not by being jealous of one another that we will come out of the difficult period we are now going through.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude on a final note that once again has to do with national unity but about which I feel very strongly. In the nearly 15 years that I have been in politics as a member of parliament, and now as a minister, I have had, of course, the opportunity to tour my country several times. I have been hoping for a long time that all my fellow citizens, particularly young people, should have the opportunity to see our country.
I am happy to see that we have several programs that allow young people to travel and know their country better. I would hope that it would be possible for older people also to use our means of communications, such as railways, to allow a greater number of Canadians to know their country better so they will love it even more and be better prepared to protect it and keep it together. The freedom to travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific without having to show a passport, the capacity to have a country that goes from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the possibility of moving from one province to another to either get treated, study, or work, all of that, Mr. Speaker, are not elements that can be accounted for. That appears nowhere in the liabilities or assets of the national accounts of both Canada and Quebec, and yet, Mr. Speaker, those benefits are real but unfortunately there is too often a tendency to forget about them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this country has more people unemployed now than it has ever had in its history. It has the highest unemployment percentage it has had at any time except during the depression years of the 1930s. Academics, business, labour and economic research institutes such as the C. D. Howe Institute and the Conference Board all called for expansionary budgets, but what they got from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was a budget which provides for no real expansion. The minister himself admits that there will be even more unemployed during 1977 than during the disastrous year of 1976.
What is the record? We have to look behind the honeyed words of the minister to find all the real facts, and they indeed show a picture of gloom and doom. In February of 1977, the last month for which we have figures, there were 932,000 people unemployed. That compares with 800,000 in February of 1976. The seasonally adjusted rate jumped from 7 per cent in February, 1976, to 7.9 per cent in February, 1977. The unadjusted rate jumped from 8 per cent in February, 1976, to 9.1 per cent in February, 1977.
Mr. Speaker, those of us who have watched the economic situation in Canada know that if you have moderate unemployment in the high growth areas, the prosperous provinces of Canada such as Ontario and British Columbia, what you have in the Altantic provinces and Quebec is economic disaster. If we look at the unemployment rates for those areas we can see that I have not exaggerated nor used inflammatory words, but am simply describing the situation as it is. In the Atlantic provinces the rate of unemployment in February, 1976, was 9.9 per cent; in February of this year it had jumped to 12.5 per cent. We know that while there still might be pretty good employment in Halifax, Dartmouth and probably St. John's, Newfoundland, what you have in places like Cape Breton and the small communities in Newfoundland is unemployment of anywhere from 30 per cent to 80 per cent.
In the province of Quebec the seasonally adjusted rate in February, 1976, was 8.4 per cent; in February, 1977, it had jumped to 9.7 per cent. In Quebec in February, 1976, 255,000 people were unemployed; in February, 1977, 303,000 were unemployed, an increase of almost 50,000.
Mr. Speaker, I ask today, as I have on so many other occasions, are we surprised that so many people in Quebec voted for a party whose major objective is the separation of that province from the rest of Canada? Should we be surprised that so many voted that way, or should we not be surprised that so many still voted for parties which believe in a federal state? Given the disinterest and lack of concern on the part of this federal government with the situation in Quebec, is it any wonder that the people of Quebec, particularly the young, turned to the separatist party in increasing numbers?
Let us keep in mind that of the 930,000 who were unemployed in February, almost half-429,000-were in the age group 15 to 24. Is it any wonder that the people of Quebec

April 5, 1977

have turned to a separatist party? What did the Minister of Finance tell them in the budget speech? What did he say last Sunday in the television program "Question Period"? What did the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) say last night in this budget debate? He said the government is not doing anything more about unemployment because they cannot afford to. I have here a newspaper report of his speech and 1 think it quotes him exactly. In the Ottawa Citizen of April 5, the minister is quoted as follows:
"Nobody, I am sure, would suggest that these billions should be found by cutting out other federal programs which are so important to our economic and social well-being," Cullen said.
"Nor could we add the vast sums which would be required to existing governmental expenditures.
The second paragraph of the article reads as follows:
Even to reduce the unemployment rate to four or five per cent from the current seasonally-adjusted national average of 7.9 per cent "would cost literally billions."
1 had talked about numbers, Mr. Speaker, but what does it mean to people to be unemployed? Any newspaper in any part of Canada will give a report of what is happening. The Globe and Mail of March 17 had a report from London, Ontario, which read in part as follows:
Keith Gibbons is one of hundreds of young people who graduated from teachers' college last year and couldn't find a job. It wasn't for lack of effort. He sent out 150 applications for jobs within a 40-mile radius of London, where his wife is a law student. "But 1 only got three responses, and out of that, only one interview."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How can the government make extra jobs for teachers?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary asks how the government can make extra jobs for teachers. It is a very good question. Probably the Department of Manpower and Immigration should have consulted with provincial governments several years ago to see whether it was necessary to train as many teachers as we have. When I came to parliament we were getting annual reports from the Economic Council of Canada telling us that in order to meet the needs of modern society we had to give the labour force a better education. Mr. Speaker, we have the best educated corps of unemployed in the world. That is what we have done with our Manpower training programs and our educational system.
A report in the Globe and Mail of March 21, 1977, date-lined Dover, Newfoundland, began this way:
Even in a province where unemployment gallops along consistently at more than double the national average, this peaceful Bonavista Bay community of 947 souls is something of an anomaly.
An incredible 80 to 85 per cent of the able-bodied men in this picturesque, ocean-side hamlet are on the dole-far and away the highest unemployment rate per capita in Canada-and between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the residents are on welfare.
I do not say that I have an answer for the people of Dover, Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker. I do not say we can find a job for every person who graduates from teachers' college, but I would not have given the university students of Toronto the answer the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave them a few days ago. The report in the Globe and Mail of March 25-
____ 4661
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Even the students did not take that as authority.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope they did not take the Prime Minister as an authority, either. He has not issued any denial of the report which reads as follows:
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau has told a group of startled university students that if they are dissatified with job opportunities in Canada they should go to another country.
The newspaper further quotes him as saying:
"We're not going to put millions into subsidization of university graduates because they have a bleak view of their future," he said.
"And if they don't like it here, let them find another country where they could use university graduates, and if they can't use them anywhere else it s because there are too many university graduates ..."
There may be too many university graduates, but one could hardly blame the students now in universities who were pretty well assured by the adult population and politicians of all parties that there would be jobs for them. We are now in almost the same situation, in terms of percentages of the available work force which is unemployed, as we were, not in 1933 at the height of the depression but in the years 1937-38. At that time members of parliament like the then member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), Mr. Woodsworth, and the then member for Winnipeg North, Mr. Heaps, said that we did not need to have the hundreds of thousands unemployed that we had, and that there was work that needed to be done. What was the answer then? It was that we did not have the money to put people to work. That was the stock answer in the 1930s. Then something happened in 1939.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was called a war.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. Suddenly there was work for all who wanted it. The government was willing to spend money on weapons which destroyed other people, but not on things which people needed. Lo and behold, at the end of the war even the Liberal government of the day, headed by Mr. Mackenzie King and guided by a tremendously competent businessman, C. D. Howe, realized suddenly that with planning the needs of the Canadian people could be met: everyone could be put to work. We accepted the idea of full employment in this country. For many years, until the early 1970s, the Economic Council, members of which were appointed by Liberal governments, sometimes by Conservative governments, said we could have full employment in this country-if one defines full employment as an unemployment rate of 4 per cent. Now that our unemployment rate is 2'/2 times greater we are being told a number of different things by some so-called experts. Full employment is now attained, apparently, when our unemployment rate is 6 per cent, not 4 per cent. Unemployment is not as bad as it was in the 1930s. After all, we have unemployment insurance and welfare and no one is starving these days. 1 hope no one again will starve in this country.
We are told that a 9 per cent unemployment rate is not serious because almost half the unemployed are women. It is assumed by some that women do not count, that they are only

The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
working to augment their husbands' income or because they want luxuries. That is the rationale of government economists.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what you hear from the Conservatives.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Conservatives on both sides of the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The former head of the Economic Council used to rationalize in that way. I suggest that women, married or not, work because they must, because their income is needed to maintain a decent standard of living. If a family wants to buy even a modest house, a woman's income is essential. Do hon. members not realize how much houses cost these days? I suppose 90 per cent of this country's families need two incomes if they arc to afford a house, a car, a holiday or any other large item. This applies especially to young married couples.
The Minister of Finance, on the program "Question Period" on Sunday night, and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in his speech last night said that we must endure present levels of unemployment because we cannot afford to put people back to work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. member opposite says that is not true.
I suggest it is true, because the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, and his statement was repeated by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, that in 1977 our labour force will grow by 250,000 persons. The Canada Works, Young Canada Works and other programs the government announced, plus the additional $100 million the Minister of Finance mentioned in the budget, will create 50,000 new jobs at best. The Minister of Finance estimated that the private sector of the economy will provide jobs for 150,000 people. I suggest the minister was too optimistic. He was too optimistic in his budgetary forecasts last year, and too optimistic when he spoke last week.
Let us assume the minister's estimates are right. The minister says the private sector will provide 150,000 new jobs, and the government's job creation programs additional jobs for
50.000	people. According to my arithmetic, that adds up to
200.000	new jobs. Yet departmental economists estimate that
250.000	people next year will join the work force. Therefore, according to the government's own figures, in the coming year unemployment will rise by 50,000 persons.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figure will be closer to 100,000.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The conference board, which is not composed of wild-eyed radicals, estimates that our growth this year will be closer to 3.5 per cent, not the minister's estimate of 4 per cent. They estimate that the private sector will provide substantially fewer than 150,000 new jobs and that the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for 1977 will not be 7 per cent, as it was in 1976, but 8 per cent. Economists with whom I have been in touch in recent years and whose estimates have been

April 5, 1977
much closer to the mark than those of the government calculate that our unemployment rate is likely to be, not 8 per cent, as the conference board estimates, but 8.5 per cent. If the U.S. economy does not pick up-and it is not picking up at the rate calculated by the American government-our seasonally adjusted unemployment rate will be closer to 9 per cent.
Clearly, we are talking about one million unemployed in 1977, even if one accepts official figures. Even then, we are ignoring the hundreds of thousands of young people who have tried time and again, unsuccessfully, to find jobs, of people who cannot get jobs because there are none, of people in the maritimes, the interlake area of Manitoba and northern Ontario who know there are no jobs to be had and know it is useless looking for work. But, says the government, "We cannot afford to do more. We cannot afford to pump more than an extra $100 million into job creation." It forgets what it did in those terrible days of 1971 and 1972 when, according to the Leader of the Opposition, the minority government was doing terrible things. He did not specify, because I suppose he did not want to say that he thought increasing and indexing old age pensions was a bad thing, increasing the Canada Pension Plan was bad, increasing and indexing family allowances was bad. Yet these things were done under a minority government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't forget veterans' pensions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, they were increased and indexed. Apparently the Leader of the Opposition thinks those accomplishments of the minority parliament were terrible. Well, in those terrible days when our unemployment rate was 6.2 per cent, not 7.9 per cent, the government was persuaded to spend $500 million on a capital works program. To put people back to work it made $500 million available to provinces and municipalities for needed works projects. Today, however, we are told that we cannot afford to spend more than $100 million which the government has put into job creation. We cannot afford to spend more than the $100 million of this total $350 million which has been allocated for job creation. As a result of the one million unemployed we will lose as of this year, 1977, $8 billion in gross national production. This means that in each of the years 1976 and 1977 government revenues will be less than they could have been, by $1 'A billion.
Because we have one million unemployed we will spend $3 billion in this coming year to prop up the unemployment insurance system and on welfare payments to people who should be working. I cannot think of anything less useful or more wasteful and degrading than spending money in that way. What does the government intend to do with these one million unemployed? They say they cannot find money to put these people back to work, despite the fact that industry is operating at 80 per cent capacity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Sixty per cent in the Atlantic region.
April 5, 1977

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government says we cannot afford to start up needed projects such as new sewer and water systems in our expanding cities, modernizing hospitals, some of which are more than 100 years old, rebuilding schools in the core area of our cities, and dealing with the problems of native people who are becoming more and more desperate. But the government says that it will encourage industry to modernize. If industry will modernize, they will give them over $1 billion in the year 1977. They do not have money for job creation, but for tax relief in respect of business inventories they have $300 million. For federal investment tax credits there is $485 million; for enhanced depletion for high-cost oil and gas wells, $20 million. For increased dividend tax credits there is $120 million, and for an increase in limit for capital losses there is $45 million. The government will not tax capital gains at the full rate, but for capital losses there is $45 million.
For inclusion of capital gains on Canadian securities there is $10 million. For other corporate and investor tax concessions, $100 million, and for losses in provincial revenues related to above, $165 million. That totals a cool $1,245 million. Again we get from this government, "To those who have shall be given."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the Liberal motto.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has been the Liberal motto for many years. There is no reason for the rate of unemployment we have in this country. There is only one other country in the western world which has anywhere near the rate of Canada. That is our neighbour to the south. From reading the newspapers it appears that Great Britain may go bankrupt, if not today then certainly tomorrow or early next week. However, even though it is in these dire straits the unemployment rate there is about half the rate in Canada.
This government has failed again. This is a cruel, callous and needless budget. Instead of dealing with the problem of unemployment it has again concentrated on the myth that we can and need to deal with inflation. For reasons which had nothing to do with the anti-inflation program, reasons beyond the control of this government, because the price of food did not rise at the rate it had been rising, the cost of living last year increased by only 6.2 per cent. The government took a great deal of credit for that. We said that credit was undeserved. This year they will have to take the blame, probably undeserved, for a much larger increase. Food and fuel prices are rising sharply. The minister will permit a $2 a barrel increase in the price of oil in the very near future. I predict that in 1977 the cost of living will increase between 8 per cent and 9 per cent. The misery index in this country, to coin a phrase, the total of inflation and unemployment, will increase next year to 20 per cent if one calculates the rate of unemployment and the rate of inflation. That is the result of having a Liberal government with its antiquated economic ideas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) gave an excellent analysis of the deficiencies of the government and the chaotic consequences of its economic policy. It is indeed hard to follow such a laudable effort. However, it was followed today with a contribution by our leader which will go down as one of the good speeches in this House, one of the critical speeches in this House, one that indicates without doubt that he has a conception of what Canada needs and a conception which the government of Canada lacks. He showed beyond a doubt that he is of a calibre to more than replace the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to take over the leadership of Canada in a constructive and beneficial way.
There are, however, a few things which remain unsaid. There appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 1 a graph recording the surplus and deficit position resulting from government budgets from 1955 to 1974. It would be difficult to give a more graphic picture, a more understandable picture of the results of the economic and monetary policies followed by this government and the long-term position in which it places the taxpayers.
This graph shows that from 1955 to 1974, a twenty-year period, the net budgetary deficit was $6,163 million. In 1978 the cash deficiency of this government will be $6,400 million. In other words, in Fiscal year 1978 we will go further into the hole than we did in the twenty-year period from 1955 to 1974 inclusive. In the budgets of 1974 to 1978 inclusive, the aggregate deficit in that five-year period is three times that of the aggregate deficit of the twenty-year period from 1955 to 1974. It would seem to me that this government has given Canada quite a push down an otter's slide of economic disaster.
The government either has been absolutely incompetent in its prediction of cost programs, as one piled upon the other, or it has decided to curry favour and to hold power regardless of the cost to the taxpayer and regardless of the ultimate economic consequence to this nation.
The multibillion dollar error made when the revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act took place is a prime example. There was no emergency provision in that act for there being a million people unemployed in Canada. There was no historic examination of the cyclical nature of worldwide income. It is obvious that it was not there. It was just assumed that the all-powerful government was capable of controlling the economy. It ignored history. It has been proven that it was as false an assumption then as it would have been at any other point in time in economic history.
The government may make a contribution by sound and solid economic policies, but it cannot reverse the trends once they have been created. No matter how this budget is examined, it does not qualify within the guidelines established by the government's anti-inflation policy. The nation must have been beguiled, mesmerized or plainly deceived in the election of 1974. Hon. Robert Stanfield had the courage to face the people of Canada with a policy that he recognized might not

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. McCain
be popular. He was convinced it was a policy that was necessary to dispel the inflationary expectations of that day. He lost the election to that beguiling and charismatic government which is presently in office, which in turn adopted a plan, though similar in name to wage and price controls as proposed by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), was at best a hybrid, mongrel version of his plan. It has not, and will not, accomplish the goals necessary to stabilize our economy. It contained absolutely no incentive for labour to become more productive, for industry to become more productive, for industry to be able to reduce margins, for industry to reduce prices as a result of the co-operative productivity effort of management and labour. It put nothing in to give anybody any desire to do a better job. It put the brakes on wages, profits and development.
It operated on the policy that profit is evil and productivity is undesired. It was not accomplished by leadership of government; it was not accompanied by an educational program; and it did not explain to Canadians the situation in which they found themselves. I have great confidence in the mass of Canadians, confidence which the government lacks. Within the memory of many people in this House, a U.S. president by the name of Roosevelt led his country. He spoke to his people explaining the situation, first at home during the thirties and the depression, and later the situation as it existed abroad as we passed into a war in which it was inevitable that the United States would have to become involved. It was unpopular to tell the people of the United States any of the facts in either of these situations. Mr. Roosevelt, calmly, slowly and openly adjusted the people of the United States to the situation in which they found themselves and prepared them for the action which had to be taken.
When one considers this example and the examples of other great statesmen of this and other countries, one realizes it has certainly been a government without courage that has governed us. It has certainly showed none of the courage of Roosevelt or other leaders. That is what this country needed above all else-good management, good leadership, good relations with the people, and good economic policies. We have lacked them all.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The cash requirement of the government has removed it from the capability of exerting an important influence upon our economy in times of emergency. The people of Canada are reconciled to the fact that perhaps this budget, under existing circumstances, has done about all that could be expected in view of the government's financial dilemma. It is incapable of exerting the effort available to a government with good management. Because of those governments which prevailed through the fifties and the sixties in this country we realize that in order to make the minimal contribution we must enter the money markets of Canada and the world, to the detriment of those who require money for development which would create employment or, worse still, the government must
[Mr McCain.]
start printing money, which would merely add to future inflation.
Government expenditures are non-productive. Private expenditures are productive. The private sphere still employs about 90 per cent of the people who work. While the government is taking an ever-increasing portion of the work force, it cannot in itself absorb a significant portion of the million people presently unemployed, nor will it be able to do so in the foreseeable future. It is in conflict with its own purposes. Only a change in government and total reassessment of public management can ever put the people in control of their own affairs.
Much of Canada's financing has been done abroad, and the present decline of the Canadian dollar, or the increasing value of certain foreign currencies would indicate that perhaps we do not yet know the consequence of living so lavishly. The Prime Minister accused the people of living beyond their means, but he did not admit that the government lived beyond the means of the people, nor did he acknowledge the consequences of it.
In 1972 a Canadian corporation floated a Swiss loan for 104 million francs. At that time they were converted into $27 million Canadian. At the existing rate of exchange the 104 million Swiss francs are worth about $43.1 million Canadian. That is the consequence of a private corporation being forced into the foreign markets to borrow, primarily because our government has absorbed so much of our own money that there is no room for the private borrower in the Canadian market.
The figure is particularly significant to the treasuries of the lesser governments of Canada than the federal government which are less capable of absorbing the losses suffered as a result of unfavourable changes in international currency. The provinces, the municipalities and publicly-owned utilities are looking at substantially increased burdens of interest and amortization costs. This is only one of the ways in which the unfavourable federal policy has exerted itself and has exerted a severely unfavourable influence upon other jurisdictions in Canada.
Realizing, too late, that the Unemployment Insurance Act was exerting unforeseen and undesirable pressures upon the treasury of Canada, we now have before the House a bill intended to reduce unemployment insurance benefits. It could not have been introduced at a more unfavourable moment in time, particularly as it relates to the less favoured areas of Canada. The vast bulk of the savings are to be at the expense of the Atlantic area and any other areas of Canada which have that burdensome 10 per cent or more of unemployment.
Every department of every Atlantic province government is struggling to stay within the guidelines of the Anti-Inflation Board. Every welfare payment estimate shows that payments will go up by not less than 20 per cent. This transfers the savings of the government of Canada at the expense of the provinces. One Nova Scotia minister, in commenting on the financial dilemma of his province in the field of welfare, has
April 5, 1977

said that the federal chickens were coming home to roost. Not in Ontario, not in Alberta, not in Saskatchewan, not even in British Columbia, but in the less favoured areas of Canada, and particularly in the Altantic area, the federal chickens are coming home to roost in more ways than one.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, responsibilities assumed by the federal government in respect of vocational training programs and for the upgrading of the qualifications of members of the work force have in the past been a very important item in our structure. They have brought about an improvement in the capability of our work force. The province of New Brunswick spent a great deal of money to establish the training centres and to equip and staff them. The government of Canada contributed to operational expenses by allocating money to applicants for courses. Recently the amount of money supplied by the government of Canada has been relatively static. While inflation has exerted its full force in the cost of materials, repairs, instructors' salaries and every possible aspect of cost, the federal contribution has failed to recognize inflationary tendencies. The province, having gone into the program in good faith, now finds itself spending money that it never anticipated would be necessary and is compelled to retract from its volume of training that had been jointly supplied.
During the winter of 1976-77 a supplementary expenditure was considered necessary for job creation through LIP programs. The moneys allocated to New Brunswick were not all absorbed by applicants at hand. The New Brunswick minister of labour asked the government of Canada to divert the excess money from LIP programs to training programs in New Brunswick. This was not acceptable to the government of Canada and $1 million once considered necessary to the economy of New Brunswick was moved elsewhere and was not used for upgrading purposes.
The economic problem is obvious and chronic, but it is beyond the capabilities of this government to recognize and resolve it. While we may not have as many votes as there are in Montreal or Toronto, we do have human beings who need to be considered in a heartfelt way. It cannot be denied that there are certain incentives in this budget which may encourage development in the poorer areas of Canada. But in his speech the minister implied, indeed said very directly, that it will take some time, a time he did not choose to define, before the effect of these incentives will become obvious. So those in areas in which the incentives have been offered are patiently to twiddle their thumbs until the magic of the Macdonald budget finally reaches out to improve their work opportunities, fully knowing that the government of Canada has wasted its substance in riotous living and is in no position to be of any real help in this time of dire need.
There was a time, Mr. Speaker, when a person might point the finger of blame at an individual cabinet minister. This is no longer the case. The Prime Minister has conducted himself in a fashion which indicates that he is quite willing to take all the credit for anything good which emerges from his government's policies, but he will sack a minister, such as Gray or Turner, Hellyer or Richardson, Marchand or Andras, if things
The Budget-Mr. McCain
do not go just right. Yet he and the 300 people in the Prime Minister's office will jealously claim all the credit.
At this point in time it is abundantly clear that experienced people are required, that ideologists are passe, that we must look reality squarely in the face and recognize that charisma will not fill lunch-buckets. This can only be done by ability, ability that is abysmally lacking in the present administration. From the Prime Minister down the Liberal party has proven to Canada that it is incapable of understanding what has happened, and therefore utterly incapable of correcting the errors of its past.
Let us make full allowance for all the outside forces which have exerted themselves upon Canada's economic affairs. These are the crutch, the excuses which one finance minister after another has used. But having done this we find foreign sources did not increase the tax burden, did not increase the monstrosity of administration which we presently have, and did not bungle the internal management of our affairs. The list of countries which have succeeded in this manner has been referred to many times during this debate. Foreign sources did not stagnate exploration and development of our energy resources, and did not lead to confrontation with the provinces. It did not irritate any ethnic group in this country. It merely provided a crutch, an excuse for this government to hold before the public, as the reason for a million unemployed in this country, that foreign influences are beyond our control. This is a deceitful approach and justifies the replacement of this government at the earliest possible moment.
Both the Minister of Finance and his critics have discounted the unfavourable balance of trade. I should like to isolate one particular aspect of our trade, namely agriculture. In 1971 the then minister of agriculture, the hon. Mr. Olson, when he addressed the Canadian Horticultural Council stated that Canada had embarked upon a "cheap food" policy, that the Canadian market would be more open to foreign sources of supply. In 1970 Canada imported approximately $1,250 million worth of food. In 1975, four years after the announcement by the then minister Mr. Olson, Canada imported approximately $2,900 million worth of food.
It must be admitted that a certain portion of our food imports cannot be controlled because there are foods which we cannot produce, but a large portion can be controlled and should be controlled. It is within Canada's horticultural capability to produce a much larger part of our own requirements. In this budget as part of the ways and means we are again faced with the reduction of duties on meats and other products at a time when our producers are already losing hundreds of millions of dollars. The cheap food policy is still in place. It is not in place for textiles, and I did not hear the consumers complain. It is not in place for other industries in Canada, and I did not hear the consumers complain either. But it is in place for food, for which Canada is famous.
There are further reductions in duties for certain food products which are competitive with fruits grown in Canada. The price of a can of orange juice will influence the consumer if it seems to be a better buy than apple juice, and this

April 5, 1977
Tabling of Documents
influence will go beyond the point of personal preference for a particular juice. It is just pure, ordinary common sense that will guide the hard-pressed consumer to the best buy on the shelf, regardless of its source of production. This, therefore, is detrimental to the interests of the average fruit producer in Canada, just as other cheap foods are detrimental to the producers of competitive products in Canada.
Not only does foreign competition from unreasonably low-cost areas take a serious toll of our farm incomes. It also eliminates this sector of agriculture as an employer from the production level right through the processing structure. We are talking in terms of tens of thousands of jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars of agricultural income. In view of the stress on our economy, it is high time that the government of Canada took a long, hard look at this as one of the points to be considered in reducing the unemployment roll, increasing the incomes of those in the agricultural industry, as well as improving our trade balance.
I have referred to increased imports of foods, Mr. Speaker. In 1971, Canadians imported $1,299 million worth of food. This was just at the beginning of the new cheap food policy. In
1972, imports increased by $239 million to $1,538 million. In
1973, imports increased by $625 million to $2,163 million. In 1974 it increased by $665 million to $2,828 million.
