subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the ten year period from 1966 to 1975 the increase in food imports was $1,855 million, or 185 per cent. That is the cost to the labour force in the farm industry, the cost to the farmer and to the processing and distribution industries which this country has experienced as agriculture has been neglected and food has been imported from abroad. We cannot tolerate this situation.
This is the situation not only so far as exotic foods are concerned; it exists also with foods with which we are quite familiar. Our imports of cherries went up by 7 million pounds in that ten year period; our imports of pears went up by 16 million pounds, plums by 16 million pounds, strawberries by 12 million pounds, apples-and this is very important-went up from 54 million pounds to 148 million pounds. That is what happens when the market is left unprotected and imports come in from areas with which we never could and never will be able to compete. We can go down the list and we find the same situation with regard to celery, corn, onions, tomatoes, and asparagus. Every one of these items was at one time important to a group of farmers in Canada but their market has been displaced by imports from outside, to the detriment of the national economy.
If we only wish to consider agriculture as an industry at home, let us give it another thought. At present we have $1 billion worth of straight surplus in agricultural products, but this has been created primarily by an increase in the volume of grain for export and also an increase in the price in the last two years which I have discussed. If at any time we have a decrease in crops or even a decrease in price, Canada will find itself, in dollar terms, in a deficient position in respect of agricultural trade. This country cannot afford that. When pressed hard enough, this country took into consideration the textile industry and acted on its behalf. I applaud the government for that action, but 1 attack it with all the strength of my heart for its neglect of Canada's food supply and of those associated with it.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Les-sard) gave a rather important speech this afternoon, but I think there are a few things of which we should become cognizant, namely, the defeating and contradictory parts of government in respect of the minister's efforts. I ask him to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) what was his position in respect of the construction of refinery structures in the oil industry on the Atlantic coast during the energy crisis. Was it constructive to the develop-
April 5, 1977

ment of those industries in that area? The answer is no, it was not. DREE moneys are being spent on the one hand and private moneys would have been spent on the other, but this was made impossible by the ridiculous regulations of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
How about the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang)? During the last session of parliament we had a bill which brought in what was known as the Maritime Code. At the same time discussions were going on for the construction of a complex for the production of steel in Sydney, Nova Scotia. The code was there. A headline in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald at that time stated "Maritime Code Detrimental to Steel Industry Development". I telephoned the president of that company, and his reply to me in respect of the Maritime Code was that if we had ever planned to build this complex in Sydney, the Maritime Code and the indecisive replies from the Minister of Transport had wiped it out because it would be cheaper to take the ore from Canada to Europe, and the coal from Cape Breton to Europe, and do the processing there, by virtue of the additional costs of sea freight alone. That was the co-operation which the Minister of DREE had from the Minister of Transport.
While he is developing industry and making his grants, what help is he getting from the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) or the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan)? What items are being purchased in the Atlantic area or in any of the depressed areas in Canada? I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) stated the case for one of his industries in a very strong and proper way last evening during the "late show". I believe that, with a little more consideration by the purchasing agencies of the government, there would not be the massive unemployment there is in the Atlantic area because there are certain items that can and should be produced there which are required by the government, and which would give a major economic lift to the area.
While the minister is making grants through DREE, does he understand the detrimental effects of poor transport policies in the Atlantic area? Is he aware of the neglect of the ports of Halifax and Saint John? Is he aware of the shortage of equipment for the movement of perishable products in that area? Is he aware of the difficulties which took place? Is he the one who influenced the expenditure of tens of millions of dollars in the Montreal area-hundreds of millions in total- on that port, while we have a study going on with regard to the port of Halifax and another being completed on the port of Saint John? We spend $10 million on a port which has reached a static level in its volume of trade and we are neglecting two Atlantic ports which have had an increasing amount of trade over the past few years. The trend is there, but the money is not. So the Minister of DREE is bucking the odds within his own cabinet. These are rather serious odds.
We heard the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) last night, and we heard comparable statements from others today complaining about the rapid increase in the work force in the last two years. They should not cry about this. Did they not have all this information at their fingertips? Did Statistics
The Budget-Mr. Faulkner
Canada not tell them 15 years ago that they would have X number of people coming in 1977 and Y number of people coming in 1978? The statistics were there, the handwriting was on the wall. It is no use making excuses in the budget introduced in 1977 for what happened and for what should have been planned in the last 15, 18 or 20 years. This is another point which was brought out by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) when he stated there is no projection of requirements for Canada, no forecast of what is coming down the road for us. We are going down a blind alley every time we get a budget.
I mentioned agriculture and the various road blocks in respect of freedom of trade which has been granted to foreigners in this country. I want to mention one other thing. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) sat by complacently while we protected the chemical industry of Canada which manufactures pesticides. The government has blocked the border so that a private farmer cannot go south to bring in his requirements. Are the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott), or the AntiInflation Board monitoring the expense that this imposes on farmers? I wonder if they care, and do they know that at least one item required by the farmers costs 50 per cent more than last year?

speechtext: Has any agency of government considered that one of the chemicals used by the potato industry from coast to coast in Canada is not available in Canada? Do they understand that this particular chemical, fusarex, puts a better quality of potato on the table, puts a better quality of potato through the processing plant, and produces a better quality of potato for the processor to sell? It is now not available at all because the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Agriculture or some other department has refused to register it, even though it is registered in the United States, is used in the United States and is needed in Canada. Where is the concern of this government for the people when it will tolerate, without any exercise of control, an increase of 50 per cent in the price of an agricultural product to protect the chemical industry while introducing in the budget, on the other hand, a list of food items, many of which we produce, and on which duties have been reduced? If ever there was a contradictory situation, the government has given us an example in this budget.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to participate in this debate, and I would like to discuss a very particular aspect of the budget and comment on the important relationship which exists between the budgetary proposals

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Faulkner
which have been introduced by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), and the government's science policy with respect to the industrial sector. Not only does the budget emphasize the importance of research and development in Canadian industry, it also provides a well rounded package of mutually supportive measures to encourage new industrial ventures, to create jobs, including jobs for highly qualified manpower, and to give special support to the new enterprises that are now getting established outside Canada's principal industrial centres.
However, before commenting in detail on those aspects of the budget that are most closely linked to the government's science policy, I would like to explain some of the circumstances which characterize the current state of science and technology in Canada.
As a nation Canada spends about 1 per cent of its gross national product on research and development. In terms of performance roughly one third of this amount pertains to government research, one third to university research, and one third to industrial research. The government is aware that Canada's national research effort is less than half that of other industrialized nations, and that the distribution of effort among the three performing sectors is the inverse of most other western nations, where typically industry performs 60 per cent of the national research effort, both internally funded and publicly funded. As I will explain shortly, the proposed budget reflects the government's intention to give greater emphasis to the research effort in industry and to design measures and policies that will encourage industry itself to take on greater responsibilities in this area.
However, more worrisome than the relatively low level of research expenditures in Canada, or the different mix of research performers, has been the recent decline in Canada's research intensity. In 1967 Canada spent 1.29 per cent of its gross national product on research and development. In 1975 this share declined to 1.1 per cent. The decline has been particularly sharp in the industrial sector, where the research intensity dropped from 1.2 per cent of sales to 0.7 per cent. As a percentage of GNP this is equivalent to a decline in the industrial share from 0.5 per cent in 1967 to 0.41 per cent in 1973. From a study which was done for my ministry we know that the decline in industrial research has been at a significantly higher rate than the over-all decline of industrial development during that period.
While I subscribe to the general thesis that a healthy industrial sector will generate enough investment funds to support an adequate level of research and development, and in do'ng so will maintain a reliable lifeline to the future, there is sufficient evidence to share the widespread concern that the current shortcomings in Canada's industrial research effort are so serious that special measures are warranted. It is for this reason that the government, through its budget which is now before us, has provided for a variety of measures to~Stimulate industrial investment in general and industrial research and development in particular. However, before describing the

economic significance of these measures, I wish to draw to the attention of the House their historic perspective.
The present state of industrial research in Canada reflects, in a way, our history as a young nation, nation rich in resources, thinly populated, close to one of the most advanced industrial nations of the world, and historically oriented toward primary industries. Because of the wealth of natural resources, Canada's first emphasis in science has been in such fields as geology, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries. In view of the national importance of resource inventories and improved farming techniques, most of these efforts started in government and have remained in government. Thus, for historical reasons, the government's own scientific activities have traditionally been the first tier in Canada's national scientific endeavour.
The second tier was built after the second world war when it became clear that Canada's post-secondary education was not up to international standards. Thus, through a system of grants and transfer payments to the provinces, the next phase of our national scientific development took place in our universities. As a result the number of Canadian universities offering post-graduate degrees has tripled over the past 30 years, and the quality of research in many Canadian universities has reached levels of international recognition. I will speak shortly about recent government decisions to maintain the level of excellence in our universities and to strengthen the granting system.
As for industry, Canada's research effort did not start seriously until the early fifties. By that time Canada's manufacturing sector had developed from an industrial policy which was based on protective customs duties on a wide range of manufactured products, open investment, and immigration. After the war, with the widespread tariff reductions which resulted from the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the general government policy to encourage the establishment of any manufacturing industry made place for more specific programs and trade agreements to assist Canadian manufacturers in adjusting to the lower tariffs and to improve the level of science and technology in Canadian industry.
However, despite these efforts, Canada's secondary industry is still lagging in productivity, and recent studies on the effectiveness of direct government grants to stimulate industrial research and development have led to the discontinuation or re-orientation of some of the direct support programs. At the same time we observe, however, that Canada has a strong international presence in such areas as mining and metallurgy, telecommunications, steelmaking, and small jet engines.
We know from many examples that Canadian industry has the capability to undertake sophisticated research and development programs, and the skills to exploit these developments in the international market. We also know that organized research and development, if successful, provides for about a 25 per cent return to a company. Yet individual companies are never certain of the ultimate outcome of research and development, and this element of risk is often cited as the reason why industry has a natural tendency to under-invest in research
April 5, 1977

and development. In Canada this tendency has recently been aggravated by corporate cash flow problems resulting from inflation and certain accounting procedures. It is for this reason that the 3 per cent inventory adjustment which is now being introduced in the budget will also be of benefit to the research effort of Canadian enterprises.
Having established a rather broadly based manufacturing industry in Canada, we are now faced with the challenge of making that sector more efficient, productive, and internationally competent. In addition we are faced with the challenge that is presented by the imbalance between a relatively well developed university sector, producing large numbers of highly qualified scientists and engineers, and the capacity of the industrial sector to absorb the entire annual crop of graduates. Under these circumstances, and certainly in times of financial restraint, the temptation exists to cut back on university support. However, such a decision would be to the long term detriment of Canada, and the government has decided to maintain a good level of university support while emphasizing the build-up of science and technology in industry. This new emphasis, which I will now explain in more detail, is a logical extension of the initial thrust of government science and of the post-war emphasis on university development.
In developing its policies to support industrial research and development, the government has been guided by four principles. First of all it was felt that the thrust of government support for industrial research should be indirect rather than direct. Such an approach not only safeguards the freedom of individual companies to make research and development decisions, but is also in keeping with the government's fiscal policy to restrain direct expenditures. Second, it was felt that government support should be sufficiently stable, and the policy sufficiently clear, to encourage companies to make long term commitments to their research and development efforts; third, that it should contribute to the creation of cash flow; and finally that it should achieve a more rapid creation of new techniques and products, which is particularly important in a high wage economy in a world where new innovations diffuse rapidly to lower wage economics.
The first approach to such indirect support has been the government policy to contract out to the private sector the research requirements of individual government departments. Under this policy Canadian industry is invited, on a competitive basis, to provide certain scientific and technological services that are required in support of government missions. Federal research contracts have increased from $18 million in 1972-73 to $86 million in the past year, and now constitute about 12 per cent of the federal research budget. Of particular interest under the contracting out policy has been the emergence of small, highly qualified, science-intensive companies, typically employing between 25 and 50 people, having annual sales of between $2 million and $5 million and excellent growth prospects.
The Budget-Mr. Faulkner
Another important feature of the contracting out policy has been the regional distribution of the science contracts. Some 30 per cent of the total contract value during 1976-77 was awarded to companies outside the principal industrial regions of Canada. The Department of Supply and Services, which is responsible for all contracting under the policy, has contributed significantly to this particular aspect of the policy by decentralizing some of its science-contract officers to Vancouver and Halifax and, more recently, to Montreal.
It is clear from our experience to date that the contracting out policy is an important mechanism to provide indirect support to industrial research and development in Canada. Already we know of major technological and commercial achievements by a number of Canadian companies that have received government research contracts, and the policy has brought government scientists in close touch with Canadian industry. Part of this initial success must be ascribed to the government decision of 1974 to encourage Canadian industry to make unsolicited proposals to government departments in order to provide even better chances for commercial spin-offs from government sponsored research. In 1976 the contracting out policy was extended to cover new as well as ongoing programs and to include other scientific activities besides research. My department, in co-operation with the Treasury Board secretariat, has now completed new guidelines and ground rules for the extended policy and these will be announced shortly.
While the contracting out policy is useful to those companies whose research and development objectives run parallel to those of government-as tends to be the case in the eletronics industry, the transportation industry, and in the general area of scientific and technical services-the policy does not offer much opportunity for companies whose research efforts do not coincide with those of government. Yet research and development is of importance to all sectors of industry, and support is needed among a broad range of companies. In order to respond to that pressing need, and in order to acknowledge and emphasize that research and development expenditures are an essential business investment in our economy, the budget proposes to extend the 5 per cent investment tax credit which is scheduled to expire on June 30 of this year, until July 1, 1980. It will also include in its coverage, current and capital expenditures on scientific research and development made after March 31, 1977, and before July 1, 1980. The extension and enrichment of the credit will mean an immediate research and development incentive of $35 million to $40 million during 1977, and the new measure will more than offset the loss of the IRDIA program which was discontinued in 1976.
By applying a three tier credit rate, the extended incentive will be of particular significance to new high technology enterprises that are getting established outside Canada's principal industrial sectors. However, the principal benefits of the proposed tax credits are expected to flow to the larger and medium size industrial research establishments in Canada. As such, the proposed tax incentive constitutes a strong and essential counterpart to the contracting out policy which has

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I was talking about the state of industrial research and development in Canada, some of the historical reasons for the pattern which has emerged in this country, the importance the government attaches to a healthy industrial research capacity, and about the major provisions within the budget which reinforce that government intention. If I may, I should like to continue my remarks and discuss several other proposals in the budget, proposals which will be of benefit to science and technology in Canadian industry.
Besides the important financial incentives for established industrial research units, the budget gives clear recognition to the importance of entrepreneurs and start-up ventures by allowing a more favourable tax treatment to stock-option plans for employees of Canadian-controlled private companies, and by allowing the deferral of capital gains taxes when the proceeds of a sale of business properties are re-invested in the same business. This measure will be important to the many small technology-based enterprises that are expanding and relocating their business.
Another supportive measure for certain technology-based enterprises is the recommendation by the Minister of Finance that certain tariff items, particularly those dealing with scientific apparatus, be referred to the tariff board for study. With the expanding capability in Canada to manufacture sophisticated instruments, it will indeed be useful to re-examine the validity of allowing duty-free entry if the goods are imported by certain qualified users.
I hope, with the introductory remarks 1 made before six o'clock, to have demonstrated that the proposed budget contains a number of measures that are an important and integral part of the government's science policy. It has aspects, Mr. Speaker, on which we have received many thoughtful submissions from the private sector, both from industrial associations and from individual companies, and I am pleased to say that the current proposals accommodate and include many of the suggestions we have received.
While the thrust of our policy is toward indirect support, which tends to put a great deal of the responsibility for the final success of industrial research and development on the shoulders of individual firms, I should point out that the government has not discontinued all of its direct support

programs. I am now referring to the highly respected Industrial Research Assistance Program, IRAP, administered by the National Research Council, to the Defence Industry Productivity Program, DIPP, administered by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and to the new Entreprise Development Program now being established by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Taken together, these programs provide some $55 million per year in the form of cost-shared development grants to Canadian industry.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, after considerable thought and discussion, and in keeping with a general policy of fiscal restraint, the government has established a clear position vis-a-vis industrial research and development in Canada. The government recognizes and acknowledges industrial research and development as an essential business investment in our economy, and the budget now before this House is a firm expression of that conviction. The measures now in place, together with the proposals in this budget, constitute a range of measures to stimulate industrial research and development in different kinds of companies and different sectors of industry.
As I explained, the contracting-out policy is certainly benefiting small and medium sized Canadian-owned firms in three specific sectors of industry. The remaining programs of direct research support will continue to be of importance to middle sized firms no longer preoccupied with the problems of survival but which have, nevertheless, difficulties in raising the full amount of money to undertake complete programs of industrial innovation. In this spectrum the proposed tax incentive and the related budget measures constitute an important incentive to encourage the larger companies, in all sectors of industry, to strengthen their research and development effort in Canada.
Before completing these remarks I wish to refer briefly to two other areas of science policy on which the government's attention has been focused recently-the university sector and the in-house research programs of the Canadian government. As we all know, there has been a great deal of anxiety among the Canadian university community about declining research grants as a result of the government restraint program. In the last few months, however, there have been three significant developments to bring this period of difficulty and uncertainty to an end.
The first of these developments pertains to our decision last November to establish the Canadian Committee on Financing University Research. This committee, which was set up after extensive discussions between the federal and provincial governments and the universities, will provide a much needed focal point to exchange information on matters dealing with university research and it will become an important mechanism for the development of recommendations on policies, programs, and procedures affecting the financing of university research. In my judgment the formation of this committee will prove to be of great significance to the federal government in its role of fostering scientific research on a national basis and,
April 5, 1977

through close co-operation with the provinces, of enhancing the national research effort.
The second initiative I would like to mention is Bill C-26 which I recently introduced in this House and which is now awaiting second reading. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the bill proposes the creation of two new granting councils and a more logical arrangement of a variety of scientific activities in government departments. To improve liaison between the three award-granting bodies, I have proposed to establish an intercouncil co-ordinating committee, made up of the three presidents of the councils and chaired by the secretary of my ministry.
As I have already explained to this House, by improving the university granting system the government wishes to express its conviction that Canada benefits substantially from the research, and that the universities must continue to provide the climate of intellectual freedom so essential to the pursuit of knowledge.
The third initiative with respect to our policies for university research is the decision, subject to the approval of this House, to increase the 1977-78 council budgets by $20 million, of which $12 million will be to compensate for the inflationary rise in the costs of research programs during the past year. This decision is in line with my earlier statement that a drastic curtailment of university funding would not be in the national interest.
In addition to this increase to offset the eroding effect of inflation, the government proposes to allocate $8 million to the granting councils with the objective to achieve greater regional balance of scientific capability, to intensify research into areas of pressing national concern, one of which was referred to by the Minister of Finance in his introduction of the budget, and to promote expanded interdisciplinary research where that is required to deal with particular Canadian problems.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to convey to you that the government's science policy with respect to the support of university research and its concomitant requirements for better federal-provincial consultation has also taken firm shape during the past 12 months.
Finally I would like to refer to the third sector of scientific performance in Canada, the government sector. With the government's decision to control expenditures has come the need to examine whether government services are indeed being carried out in the most cost-effective manner. This examination includes a study of the government's science programs and my ministry, in co-operation with the Treasury Board secretariat and the departments concerned will review the science programs in order to ensure that the programs still meet a specific need, and to determine whether the programs ought to be carried out by government or elsewhere.
At the same time we recognize that science and technology will continue to play an important part in the execution of departmental missions, and new programs of research and development have been formulated in such areas as energy, space, and the environment. As a matter of principle, however,
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
and in keeping with the government's desire to give more prominence to the role of the private sector in Canada, these new programs will be carried out with a maximum participation by Canadian industry. We believe that the ultimate diffusion of any new technology in society will be greatly enhanced when the initial research and development are undertaken with that final goal in mind.
The government has made major progress in formulating and implementing a meaningful science policy in Canada. Several of the measures that are now being proposed by the Minister of Finance form an integral part of that policy. For these particular reasons I commend the budget to the support of this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome the opportunity to speak on this latest budget. There is certainly not much to speak about, except mostly what has been left out. With the latest budget there will be no significant change on the Canadian scene with regard to high unemployment or economic resurgence.
The budget speech talks of an underlying trend to lower inflation. In fact the CPI is already moving sharply upwards. The last three months average annualized is %'h per cent. Underlying factors if anything predict a trend toward double digit inflation. These include higher import prices caused by devaluation, higher energy costs, and higher food prices.
There is no balance of payments objective and there is no government deficit objective. "But responsibility for the economy rests on others as well." The federal government is alone responsible for the money supply growth which fuels inflation.
The speech talks of responsibility also lying with the leadership of the labour movement. The budget document reveals that discussions with labour leaders have produced no voluntary wage guidelines.
The minister has forecast that 150,000 new jobs will be created. Under current economic conditions even that forecast may be optimistic. Even if the minister is correct, and he does not have a good track record, as the labour force is predicted to increase by 225,000, he is budgeting for an additional
75,000	unemployed on the average in 1977. The minister's budget is predicated on an average unemployment rate in 1977 of 7.7 per cent. That is not full employment budgeting.
The budget plans $458 million in spending to create jobs in 1977-78. However, $358 million was already a planned expenditure on job creation before this budget. The minister's policy of throwing a further $100 million at the unemployment problem is little more than spitting in the wind. It is a last ditch effort to try to disguise the fact that the budget is six months too late. All that the money they are spending on job creation will do is to reduce the rate of increase of unemployment.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) announced that there is no money for job creation programs, but lots of money to build a new park and recreation facility at Mirabel, and another federal government complex in Montreal as well as the Guy Favreau complex.
80012-17Vi

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
Families were given very little in terms of reducing the income tax burden to help them in their personal battle against inflation. Although the unemployment expense deduction was increased by $250 and the tax credit for children under 18 was increased by $50 to a total tax credit limit of $500, the real effect of the budget was to increase the total income tax burden.
Changes in the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements for various cost-shared programs mean that the federal government needs less funding and thus can reduce taxes. However, the provinces will be required to make up the difference. Thus if one looks at the tax changes on the same basis as last year, the tax burden will be increased by 16 per cent on the average. In the years of Liberal government the tax burden upon Canadian families has risen from 12.9 per cent to 18.6 per cent of total income, a real measure of the loss of control over our own income that we have suffered.
From the government which had the audacity to tell Canadians that they are living too extravagantly has come a budget that records a $7 billion deficit, up nearly 50 per cent from last year's deficit. This sum is larger than the entire budget of the last Progressive Conservative government. It is a telling indictment of a government which for so long ceased to manage that it can look upon drift as economic leadership. It appears that we are headed toward a 90 cent dollar. Currency devaluations are the market's way of telling us that the economic management of the country is failing. It is in this context that the decline in our currency's value to 95 cents U.S. is viewed not as a problem in itself but as a symptom of a serious failure in economic management.
It now appears that four root causes have reduced the buying power of our currency. First, our rate of inflation has been consistently higher than that of our major trading partner, the United States. The implicit price index for gross national expenditure rose by 9 per cent in Canada compared to 4.8 per cent in the U.S. during the year ending in the third quarter of 1976. Second, this country has seen massive balance of payments deficits. The latest deficit was $1,363 million in the last quarter of 1976, the worst in Canadian history. Third, the political climate for investment in Canada has deteriorated drastically, and not only because of the situation in Quebec. Last year direct investment in Canada fell off by $1 billion to a net outflow of that type of investment of $400 million. Fourth, Canadian productivity is lagging. As the government sector increasingly dwarfs the productive element of the economy, this problem will grow ever more acute.
Any competitive advantage that Canadian sales abroad will receive from the discount pricing of our resources and manufactured goods will be no more than temporary if no action is taken on these fundamental problems. The experience of Britain, where currency devaluation is virtually a routine affair, shows that without strong action wage and import costs soon force export prices back up to unrealistic levels. When these goods become uncompetitive, balance of payments deficits

once again begin to pile up, forcing yet another currency devaluation. Unchecked, the process is a vicious spiral which ends up in national bankruptcy.
The human cost of the inability to deal with economic basics is measured in unemployment. This month figures were released showing that 932,000 Canadians, or 7.9 per cent of the labour force, are actively looking for work but unable to Find it. Official statistics do not record the number of people who have despaired of finding a job, but when the unofficial estimates of these numbers is included in the unemployment figures the total rises to well over one million. It is a shocking figure, and when one considers the waste and futility that lie behind these statistics one sees the true enormity of the failure of those entrusted to manage the economy.
In the face of the need for reform, this year's budget was prepared once again by the same government ministers and officials in the same state of total secrecy as the budgets of previous years which served this country so badly. At the end of last month we were once again told: "Here is the economic policy, like it or lump it." What is needed is an open process of consultation and it is needed now, not at some vague point in the future.
It is now clear to many that the country is well on its way to the 90 cent dollar. We have a million unemployed. Inflation is moving upward toward double digits. It is time to acknowledge the failures of the past and begin now the reforms that will get the country moving again.
I always like to acknowledge something which is constructive, Mr. Speaker, and although there were some slight tax reductions in the budget, they were surely far from enough. A substantial cut in personal income taxes should have been made. Tax breaks are necessary to restore growth and create jobs. Innovative tax measures to encourage business to create jobs are also necessary. A reduction in government intervention in the private sector and better communications among government, labour and business would restore the confidence of investors, both Canadian and foreign, who presently are reluctant to invest because of the Liberals' economic fiasco.
The government has the most devastating and dastardly record of any government in Canadian history. In 10 years the budget has skyrocketed over 400 per cent, from $8.8 billion to a forecast $46 billion in this past fiscal year, April 1, 1976, to March 31, 1977. Total government spending per person was $2,900 in 1975, but the government took in only $2,700 per person. Thus it has proceeded to spend an additional inflationary $200 for each of us. Transfer payments of $21.4 billion represent little more than half the current budget. Of these payments, more than $9 billion went directly to Canadian citizens in social welfare expenditures such as old age security, family allowances, and unemployment insurance. The national debt of the federal government will be around $28 billion at the end of the fiscal year, the result of budget deficits in 20 of the last 23 years.
Interest on the national debt, which was already $1.2 billion in 1967, will be around $4.6 billion at the end of this fiscal year, making it the third largest federal expenditure after
April 5, 1977

health and welfare and economic development and support- all in all, a very dismal record. The government is also contracted to guarantee the borrowings of Crown corporations such as Air Canada and the CBC. Last year the government guaranteed $15.5 billion in loans and advances to Crown corporations, which are accountable to no one. Federal spending has grown faster in the past ten years than the private economy that supports it. During the last fiscal year expenditures for the Liberal government's bilingualism program reached $121 million. Federal employees, excluding the armed forces, were paid approximately $5 billion in 1975, about triple the $1.7 billion they were earning in 1965. Some record, Mr. Speaker!
I should also like to give recognition to a colleague of mine, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who has been doing a commendable job in regard to Liberal government secrecy. The hon. member has lately been doing some advertising to get the message across to the Canadian people, and has formed a league, The League to Restore Parliamentary Control. I have joined his league and I fully support it. He has advertised in newspapers across the country and the advertisement reads:
I favour action to restore parliamentary control, including:
(a)	A freedom of information law, with a review process binding on the
government;-
With this government, Mr. Speaker, such a law is badly needed. The government does not like supplying any of us with information. The ad continues:
(b)	Accountability for spending of taxpayers' money and use of delegated
power;-
We have had no accountability, or adequate accountability of taxpayers' money which has been spent since the Liberals changed the rules in 1968, reducing the number of votes and destroying the committee system. There is no accounting to parliament now regarding government spending, a matter which has been highlighted in the last number of Auditor Generals' reports.
The hon. member's ad also calls for increased independence for private members. This means more consideration should be given to private members' bills. The government is always saying that we never have any alternatives or anything constructive to offer. But every time we offer a private member's bill or a private member's motion, something constructive, we hear a "no" or it is talked out.
The hon. member for Peace River has compiled a statement on his Freedom of Information League. 1 am not going to deal with the complete statement. One point that 1 am particularly concerned about is number two on his list, and that is government accounting for taxpayers' dollars. That is the prime responsibility of any elected official, to see that taxpayers' dollars are spent properly and that there is complete accountability. There is no complete accountability with this government. Hon. members see estimates going through different departments; hon. members see items under the heading "Oth-
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
ers" have gone up $5 million, and hon. members see "Miscellaneous" has gone up $300 million. That has to be daylight robbery. It is an absolute farce and has nothing to do with accountability.
The document of the hon. member for Peace River on accountability states:
Two of the great revolts in the English speaking world ... The parliamentary rebellion against Charles I and the American revolution each had its origin in the improper taking and spending of tax money of the people.
Now we can add the Liberal government to that little historic document. The document continues:
And, now, hundreds of years later, we find we have gained nothing. In fact, we have lost much ground because of the monstrous increase in spending, the complexity of government and inability of parliament and the people to be kept advised and be aware of how much and the manner of government spending.
Starting in 1966 right through to 1972, the date of his last report, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, former Auditor General, made yearly comments about the weakening of parliamentary control of expenditure.
This means that the government does not want to be accountable and has no intention of being accountable. The document goes on:
This was not just through a philosophical statement but borne out and corroborated in each year by a number of very carefully detailed illustrations. But, nothing was done. To show it was not just one man's opinion, the present Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell, said in his last report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1976, at page 9: "I am deeply concerned that Parliament and, indeed, the Government has lost, or is close to losing, effective control of the public purse. I expressed that concern a year ago in my Annual Report stating that:-
'The present state of the financial management and control system of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below the acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.' "
Last Sunday night I saw a television program that originated in Ottawa. It was a local commentator, and he had on two Liberal backbenchers. I see one of them in the House tonight. I did not hear one comment from either one of them about being accountable. The only thing we got out of them was that if we have shorter speeches parliament will work better.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the phony applause. Shorter speeches have nothing to do with being accountable. It has nothing to do with accountability; it has nothing to do with "Others" and "Miscellaneous". They want to strengthen the committee system. Of course, that is old hat. The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) proposed that ages ago. The committee system today is an utter farce. There was nothing discussed on this television program about philosophy. I never heard anything from these two backbenchers about strengthening the accounting system or dealing with the Auditor General's report. They tried to make this sound as though it were a mutual admiration society. They never covered any of the genuine issues, real issues.
To read further from the document:
Here's the best evidence possible that not only have the people, through their parliament, been unable to deal with official spending but the government itself is largely clueless.
I do not think the government knows what is going on. I do not think it can find out. The document continues:

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
And, with this, federal public spending estimates jumped from 1971-72 to 1977-78 from $14 billion to $41 billion, and during this time the government has been engaged in an attempt to kid us all by telling us solemnly it is engaged in policies of restraint.
They do not even know the meaning of the word! It is an absolute farce. But when the two hon. members were on television, they tried to give us the impression that everything was upright and above board, and that they were being accountable and so forth.
I would like to refer to a question that I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday. It was with regard to a consultant's report received from E. P. FitzGerald & Associates in Ottawa. I asked the Prime Minister what he was going to do with this document. There are a lot of excellent recommendations in it. The Prime Minister said that I have a vested interest in this document. I never said I had a vested interest in the document. I asked him what he was going to do with that particular document. I said that it should be referred to the finance committee for study. The Prime Minister says that we have hundreds of answers and hundreds of documents. Well, what are they doing with all these hundreds of documents? This one in particular should be referred to the finance committee so that they could discuss some of the recommendations. I imagine that this document cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to be compiled. What are they going to do with it? I suppose we would never have heard anything about it if I had not obtained a copy of it.
There are some excellent suggestions in this report. As an example, it comments on the roles of government.
Whether we like it or not, government will continue to play a dominant role in managing affairs in our society. However, in order to provide the tax base necessary for the provision of services now regarded as essential, while at the same time limiting the unnecessary growth of the bureaucracy, four key elements require to be given special attention:
I would like to make one comment on the growth of the bureaucracy. We have a statement from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) that they are going to curtail the growth of bureaucracy. They have a sneaky way of getting around this. Every government department today is hiring part time and full time employees by the hundred from Office Overload agencies. The expenditure is up in the millions of dollars. The President of the Treasury Board tells us that they are cutting back, but they are using this back door method of hiring people from employment agencies. I will go into that at another time.
The E. P. FitzGerald report that was prepared for the Liberal party's "Way Ahead Program" points out:
The private sector requires to be given access to those areas where it can provide the maximum contribution in view of its flexibility and innovative capacity.
The present overlapping conglomerate of programs carried out by the various government departments, together with the under-utilization of skilled human resources in the public service, requires to be rationalized.
There is no question about that. There is tremendous duplication between federal and provincial governments. This is the first challenge that we should meet. I did not hear the hon. members discussing this on the television program

Sunday night. I heard nothing from the government about cutting out duplication.
The report continues:
The main goal here would be to minimize the waste of resources and ensure that the social levy quotient is administered with maximum effectiveness.
The potential for a positive management approach in the field of collective bargaining should be energetically pursued.
If hon. members opposite want to strengthen the committee system, this would be an excellent report to start to discuss all these points. One of the areas that I am particularly interested in-as are my colleagues in the Conservative party-is the reference in the report to reducing waste in government spending. The report goes into some detail as to how waste in government spending can be solved, as follows:
In the writer's view, based on consulting experience with a considerable number of government departments, the principal causes of waste or, more correctly, under-utilization of resources, in the federal Public Service, include the following:
(a)	Doubtful value of some programs.
(b)	Misuse of skilled human resources.
If you want to check back on previous speeches I have made, you will find I made reference to federal civil servants being paid $20,000 to $28,000 per year and claiming that they worked only about two hours a week. What are the backbenchers doing about this? They will do nothing.
The report goes on to read:
(c)	Excessive bureaucracy of the personnel administration system.
(d)	Dehumanization of the work content of routine jobs, e.g. compilation of pay.
(e)	Over zealousness in the secondment of senior line management on task force projects.
(0 Confusion as to the roles of Treasury Board, Public Service Commission and departments in the administration of programs.
(g)	Second language requirements for employees over 50 years of age.
(h)	Policy decisions taken by senior management which are properly the responsibility of the Liberal party.
If we are going to strengthen parliament and the committee system, this would be an excellent document with which to start. The Prime Minister says they have hundreds of them. I do not know why we need hundreds of them; they probably all say the same thing. Let us start with this one because the Prime Minister has his hands on this document.
A recent article entitled, "Debt Service Costs for Governments up 120 per cent in Five Years", an unbelievable record for the government, states the following:
The annual cost to the Canadian taxpayer of government debt has risen to $822.92 per person employed in the country, up from $444.44 five years ago.
These amounts represent the interest payments made on direct government debt in the fiscal year ending this month, compared with the 1971-1972 fiscal year.
Total debt service payments made out of tax revenues by federal, provincial and municipal governments during the past year amounted to $7.9 billion, up 120 per ce it from five years earlier.
This growth rate was much faster than the five year increase for the average weekly industrial wage (65 per cent) or the consumer price index (55 per cent).
April 5, 1977

The figures were obtained from Statistics Canada, federal Treasury Board and Bank of Canada publications.
The debt service costs reflect all interest paid on direct debt incurred by all levels of government in Canada.
All in all it is a very dismal record.
One of my main concerns and my colleagues' concern is the future of small and medium sized businesses which are being regulated to death, taxed to death, and swamped with government rules and regulations, but they are the backbone of Canada. Small is beautiful. This phrase sums up the heart of the fundamental political force of this decade-the fight against bureaucracy. This struggle which has dominated the political fabric of western industrialized nations, notably in the recent past in the U.S. and Sweden, is a battle not so much against government as for liberty.
The government does not appear to realize in any meaningful way that the survival of small business is linked to the survival of the mixed economy. Despite the fact that between 50 and 60 per cent of Canadians are employed by small and medium sized businesses, little more than half-hearted solutions have been produced by the federal government. The newly created Department of State for Small Business is seen by many as paralleling the Department of Multiculturalism which appeared briefly before the 1974 election as a sop to dissatisfied voters and then, the election having been won, vanished. After listening to the unsatisfactory answers of the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand), one wonders how much longer he will last.
The Minister of State for Small Business cannot exist for long in a policy vacuum without succumbing to the same fate as his multicultural predecessor. What is needed is a strong and innovative small business policy which should consider very actively allowing tax credits for investment in small business; providing assistance in the formation of small business export consortia; changing government tender practices so that small businesses supply a greater portion of government purchased goods and services; and reducing the government paper work burden imposed on small business.
I understand the minister has announced he will be removing some of the paper work. We will be watching very closely to see if it happens.
The small and medium sized business sector cannot take much more official hesitation and vacillation. Government ministers and bureaucrats have only a short time left to learn that the problems of small and medium sized businesses are not just the problems of small businessmen but are the problems of Canada as a whole.
We in the opposition are criticized from time to time for not having alternative proposals, but I think one of the most positive questions we have asked is whether we really need 29 ministeries in Canada.
