speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to speak in the budget debate and to point out some of the measures which apply to South Western Nova. At a time when we asked people to restrain their spending and when we worked under the Anti-Inflation Board, we could not have expected a spending budget, much as I myself could see many areas of need in South Western Nova where money could be spent.
However, in these times when unemployment and business growth are problems facing any government, whether it be municipal, provincial or federal, we must look again at our priorities and reconsider where and how our dollars are being spent. This challenge, as I said, goes not only to governments but to the people and to business. Nothing should be spent without considering why we are spending the money and what it will create.
The anti-inflation program has been successful. It has kept the expectations of the Canadian people down and has allowed everyone to reconsider what are the priorities for Canada and what the mode of living of the people will be once the controls are lifted. In my opinion, the anti-inflation program has already been successful. The value of real income has risen strongly over the past 18 months. Wage settlements have come into line with the actual output of production. Certainly productivity is a word which seems to be returning to the vocabulary. One other factor has been that unions and workers are now emphasizing other conditions, such as working conditions, as an important part of a wage settlement.
The opposition is asking us on the one hand to spend, and on the other hand is criticizing us for spending and for creating inflation. We have to keep the rate of inflation down if we are to get a true picture of the Canadian economy.
I am pleased to see the value of the Canadian dollar decline. In South Western Nova we export most of our fish to other countries. The decline in the value of the dollar will help in the export of fish, as well as in other exports. The decline of the dollar will also help the tourist industry which is very important to the economy of South Western Nova and other areas in Nova Scotia. For whatever reason, whether it was the Olympics, the U.S. bicentennial or the increased value of the Canadian dollar last year, the tourist industry in South Western Nova and Nova Scotia certainly suffered. I hope that the decline in the Canadian dollar will encourage tourists to come back this year. I realize that Nova Scotia is an attraction on its own, but sometimes other incentives are needed.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has stated, this is a critical time. It is a time for us to persist in maintaining our efforts to lower inflation while we pursue steady growth in the economy. Capital investment is weak, and we need to improve our export markets as well as growth in business investments. This is a challenge not only to the government but also to the public. The programs we have under DREE, the Federal Business Development Bank and small business loans should all be utilized to the fullest extent,

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Miss Campbell
although I must put myself on record as being opposed to a great deal of the red tape small businesses, particularly in my area, must go through just to qualify or to see if they qualify.
I would like to discuss a few matters of concern to the east. With regard to energy, within the last few months the federal government has announced assistance to the governments of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. This assistance was very much needed. People are being encouraged to take part in energy conservation by insulating their homes. I am still a firm advocate of looking to our renewable resources as sources of energy; however, I would like to see the establishment of an international grid system which would be controlled by the federal government and over which no one province would have control.
The sources of power at Churchill Falls, Gull Island and James Bay are the cheapest sources of power for the east, and they are the quickest to get at and use. Let us hope that the Maritime Energy Corporation takes strong action in this direction.
I do not wish to spend too much time on this, but I think that praise and thanks to the rest of Canada, which recognizes the plight of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, are now due. I am sure that the eyes of most of the countries of the world are looking to see what will develop in terms of Nova Scotia's energy problem.
I would now like to turn to the matter of job creation. As the House is aware, I spoke last week on the unemployment insurance amendments contained in Bill C-27. I am pleased to note in the budget the additional amount of $100 million for job creation. This money can now go to create real jobs, and perhaps we should start by looking at the job creation program. I myself would like to see projects developed which will create jobs for the group which will be looking for extra weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits and which will also be looking for work because of the decreased benefit period. This is what we consider the target group. This is the group which will be most affected by the unemployment insurance amendments contained in Bill C-27.
Let us hope that this $100 million will create real and long-lasting jobs. In addition, I think the public should be challenged to create new jobs. Perhaps there are people who have projects which, if provided funds for employing people, could be successful and create new jobs.
Although I am concerned about our unemployment problem, I must say that this government has been good for Nova Scotia, and particularly South Western Nova. During my brief stay here in Ottawa as a member of parliament I have seen changes. The Princess of Acadia has been taken over by East Coast Marine Services. It was initially purchased by the federal government in 1974 from the CPR, but in the fall of 1976 it was taken over by East Coast Marine. However, I have not seen the Bluenose replaced, and I am still hoping to see that. I realize that there have been difficulties in that another competitive firm has been operating out of Yarmouth to Maine. However, I did see the Marine Cruiser come in this winter when there was no other service to handle the heavy

traffic. I look forward in the near future to seeing a replacement for the old Bluenose.
I would like to mention the physical distribution centre. This is helping all businesses in the maritime provinces from its outlet in Moncton. However, we are still obtaining goods from Ontario and Quebec markets which are far too expensive. I look forward to seeing new ideas developed so that there can be a decrease in freight rates. Perhaps what is required is business people getting together, or perhaps counties or provinces should get together to try to bring freight rates down.
Again with regard to transportation, at Digby we have a new 3,000 foot airport. I call it an airport, although we are still looking for much more development. There is a 3,000 foot paved strip. This was brought about as a result of a joint effort by the municipality of Digby, the province of Nova Scotia and the federal government.
We are asked on many occasions to discuss at random different things at different times on different bills. I am pleased that the budget allows a member of parliament to discuss how government programs affect constituencies such as mine.
I look forward to seeing greater expansion of our fishing industry in our new 200 mile jurisdiction. We now have jurisdiction over the fishery, and I do not think other countries will allow us to waste this needed food resource. I hope our fishing boats will be able to harvest the fish and also that our plants will be able to process the catches. This is a great challenge to South Western Nova and to the rest of the province.
Other aspects of the fishing industry have been improved as well. In the summer of 1976 a building worth approximately $1 million, the Environment Building in Yarmouth, was opened. This building is part of the federal government program to bring needed services to the people. It will provide to fishermen and to the industry all the information required which, prior to this office being opened, had to be obtained from the Halifax regional office.
Wharves in South Western Nova are gradually being fixed up or replaced. There have been three multi-million wharves either started or opened during my time here as a member of parliament. They are at West head, Yarmouth and Meteghan. Work has been done in other areas such as Tiverton, Cape St. Mary, Pinkney's Point and Sluice Point, and I look forward to seeing wharves in other areas worked on this year.
On February 2, 1976, we experienced what was called the ground hog day storm. High tides and wind created a considerable amount of damage to existing wharves. Under an agreement between the federal government and the provincial government of Nova Scotia, the Emergency Measures Organization spent several million dollars in South Western Nova to help rebuild such areas as Westport and Freeport in order to re-establish the fishermen who suffered losses in the storm and to finance municipal, provincial and federal losses. The money certainly did not cover the total loss, but it was
April 5, 1977

intended to restore the economic balance of all the communities involved.
The Federal Labour Intensive Projects Program has been used at the two bases in my constituency. CFB Cornwallis received approximately $104,000 and CFB Barrington received approximately $24,000. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Nothern Development (Mr. Allmand) was able to provide last year, again under the Federal Labour Intensive Projects Program, the amount of $100,000 to help create seasonal employment at Kejimkujik National Park. This year a post office will be built in Clementsport. 1 am looking forward to programs for the Annapolis Valley Tourist Association coming forth to replace some of the industries that have suffered in the Annapolis area. These are just a few of the areas about which this government has shown concern.
I should like to return to the budget and speak of another area that I thought was a step forward. This measure was taken to encourage investment and regional growth. It was a recognition by this government that perhaps certain areas should be treated differently from the rest of Canada. We see this with the investment tax credit which will be extended for an additional three years at 5 per cent for most of Canada. The credit will be increased in slower growth areas designated under the Regional Development Incentives Act. Saskatchewan, Manitoba, northern Ontario and designated regions in Quebec will go to a tax credit of IVi per cent, while the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe region will go to a tax credit of 10 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A useless policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not see it as useless, Mr. Speaker. I look forward in the future to more of this type of measure. If we are to keep Canada together we have to recognize that some areas need more help at times than other areas, and vice-versa. Perhaps hon. members who come from well-to-do areas will some day be in the same boat and need a little of that help.
There are other tax changes which I am sure are of concern to my area. The sales tax exemption for small manufacturers will be increased from $3,000 to $10,000. The government also intends to exempt certain producers of craft products which are of significance to Canadian culture and heritage. Consultation with the crafts industry will be necessary, we are told, before determining which groups will be exempted. Small crafts people in South Western Nova as well as Nova Scotia should be happy to hear of the sales tax exemptions, as will some of the culture and heritage crafts people.
Other measures and programs are going to be introduced to ease the cost of conversion to the metric system. This can only help small businesses in my area.
Income tax measures will be introduced to help working Canadians on modest incomes. Parents will be able to claim an additional $50 tax credit for each dependent child under 18 years of age resident in Canada, up to the maximum of $500
The Budget-Mr. Darling
which is the present limit. The employment expense allowance will be increased to $250, effective for 1977. At the present time it is 3 per cent of wage and salary income to a maximum of $150. These two measures combined will eliminate tax for a married taxpayer with two children earning less than $7,360, of whom there are a good many in my area, and for a married taxpayer with four children the ceiling will be $8,295.
Perhaps spending was restrained in this budget, Mr. Speaker, but there is a lot more in it that can help the people of Nova Scotia and South Western Nova if they wish to take advantage of government programs. They are invited to participate and help in the continuing fight against inflation, and also to look forward to the time when controls are lifted and to participate in growth and regional investment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on his decision to step down at an early date as I understand that this is his last budget. One look at the budget is enough to convince most observers that the minister has waited too long to step down. With the largest cabinet in the history of Canada, and indeed the largest cabinet in any country in the western world, it is becoming more and more difficult for reasonable and intelligent Canadians to believe that this budget is the best that our government can produce. Surely 32 cabinet ministers and a veritable army of bureaucrats and economic experts can come up with a better budget than this thing we are debating today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Darcy McKeough?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hear my shy and bashful friend from Nickel Belt asking about Darcy McKeough, but I understand his budget has not been presented yet.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is going to be a carbon copy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will see what comes from it. We are debating the budget that was brought down on Thursday evening, and in all frankness I think we would have been wiser if things had been reversed and those of us who wished to make suggestions had been able to do so prior to the budget. Maybe the minister would have taken some of our suggestions rather than just going his own sweet way with his bureaucrats and officials conjuring up the present budget.
One of the first remarks I heard when the budget was being read was that it certainly did not sound like an election budget. We can be sure of that, despite the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announcing this afternoon that six by-elections will be held on May 24, Queen Victoria's birthday. Neither is this a budget that will provide jobs for the more than one million unemployed. It is not a budget that will inspire the confidence of investors, and it is not a budget that will get our sluggish economy moving again. Those are the things that we have been expecting in a budget, things that are badly needed, and yet provision was not made for them. I have to ask, then, what was the point in tabling a budget in the first place?
4678

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Darling
I think the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) put his finger on the real purpose of this budget when he labelled it a survival budget-but not the survival of the working people of our country, nor the survival of our traditional way of life. It was surely nothing more or less than the survival of the government for the time being.
The Minister of Finance said that the government would be compelled to borrow an additional S6V2 billion in the coming year to finance the provisions in this budget. I think that is the real nub of this budget. When you weigh the advantages in this budget against the cost to the people, it is easy to see that it is directed at the welfare of the government rather than the welfare of the people.
The government even plans to rob the dead in order to raise a few more pounds of flesh, Mr. Speaker. It is pretty difficult for the dead to rise up and speak out against the ravages of this hungry and rapacious government, and the Minister of Finance knows that on that score he is on firmer ground with those who are grief-stricken by the loss of a loved one. I am speaking of the government's plan to tax the proceeds from insurance policies. Insurance policies on individuals are intended to pay the cost of the funeral of the deceased and to help ease the financial plight of those left behind. Traditionally these insurance benefits have been left alone by all previous governments, but not by this government. This government can spot a good thing when it sees it, especially if there is a chance to grub a few more dollars from the Canadian taxpayers. I think in that particular measure we have reached the low point in taxation policy, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance, however, missed another good deal when he was searching for new ways to raise ready cash for his spendthrift departmental bureaucrats. He overlooked the fact that many people have gold teeth and bridgework. I believe one other government tried to raise money by that horrible procedure.
There is another kind of taxation which makes me wonder how far the government will go in taxing our people. It is something that was left out of rather than included in the budget. I had hoped to find provision in the budget for the removal of that insidious ten cents per gallon federal tax on gasoline-that extra tax imposed on gasoline in July, 1975. Answering a question I asked a few days ago, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) told me the government has raised $1,025,570,000 from that ten cents per gallon gasoline excise tax during the past 15 months. Since this is money the government had not collected previously, it must be considered as gravy. Why then should it be necessary to try to grub additional money through taxes at this time, by taxing proceeds from personal insurance policies and life insurance policies?
To begin with, the gasoline taxes impose an extra and unnecessary burden on those same people, those in the lower income brackets, because many people must use their automobiles to get to and from their jobs. Those people seem to be the first target of the Minister of Finance when he is instructed to

raise more money. In the case of the gasoline excise tax, the government has raised over $1 billion.
There is another side to the extra tax on gasoline. It discourages people from travelling in their own country and discourages people in the United States from driving to Canada for their vacations. My own area, Parry Sound-Mus-koka, depends to a large extent on tourism to balance its economy over the year. When tourism in Canada suffers, especially in Ontario, my area suffers. Mr. Speaker, I find myself fighting against stupid government policies at the same time as I try to encourage tourists to come to Parry Sound-Muskoka. It actually appears to me at times as if the government is doing everything it can to make it difficult for tourism to flourish in this country, or even survive. I believe figures for 1976 show that Canada had a deficit in tourism of over $1 billion. Even though we are considered as an important tourist area and have attracted people from the United States as well as from other parts of the world, we ran up that huge deficit.
Speaking of tourism, let me be parochial and speak of a letter which was referred to in a weekly newspaper, the Haliburton County Echo of March 30, 1977. The letter referred to was written by Mr. George Tawse-Smith, director of marketing for the Canadian Office of Tourism. It was a form letter which had been sent to American Fishermen, and was addressed to "Dear Angler". The letter for the first two pages explained the many advantages of coming to Canada, to go fishing. It then went on to say, as reported in the newspaper, the following:
... "Canada offers the fisherman such a vast choice, it's hard to decide where to go. Let me make a suggestion ... just across our neighbourly border lies the finest fishing paradise you could imagine-in "La Belle Province du Quebec".
The letter then goes on for a further page to expound the fishing advantages of the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no quarrel with the tourist industry, or with the fishing industry in Quebec. I am told there are many other parts of Canada where the fishing is just as good and, to me, that letter was discriminatory. I point out that the department responsible for tourism is responsible for attracting tourists to Canada, but not to any one particular spot in Canada. It is up to individual provinces to do their best to invite tourists, and to make particular areas within provinces as attractive to tourists as possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is great fishing in Hamilton Bay.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but can you eat the fish?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have lots of good fish in Nickel Belt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the Red Baron of Nickel Belt saying there is good fishing in his area. Mr. Speaker, there is good fishing in Parry Sound-Muskoka, and in many places in northern Ontario.
Along with tourism, one of my major areas of interest is small business. Mr. Speaker, small business provides more
April 5, 1977

than 50 per cent of all jobs in Canada. That is why I find it difficult to understand government policy on this important sector of the Canadian economy. Although it must be admitted that this budget makes a start in the direction of recognizing the importance of small business, it falls far short of doing what it needed. For one thing the budget is worded in such a way that the government can squirm out of its commitments in this case, just as it did with the budget of the Minister of Finance ten months ago. A number of promises in the last budget were not honoured, and others were implemented in a different way than we had been led to expect. 1 am afraid that some of the fuzzy and nebulous provisions of this budget for assisting small business will end up on the cutting room floor.
The time lag between the tabling of the budget and legislation flowing from it is such that the government can dream up all kinds of excuses, and usually does. Sometimes we are told that, in the meantime, things have changed and measures proposed in the budget are no longer appropriate. Therefore we get nothing. On other occasions we are told there is no money to implement other proposals in the budget, and again we end up with nothing. Or at best we get a watered down version of what we were led to expect. The plain fact is that we must stop spending billions of dollars on patched-up measures and put the money where it will produce long-term employment.
A few thousand people in Canada will be pleased to learn that they have been selected to participate in Canada Works and Young Canada Works projects, and that they will be able to work for a couple of months and make a few hundred dollars. For people who simply cannot find any kind of job, it is better than nothing at all. For that reason alone I can go along with the expenditure of $452 million in the coming year for make-work projects. However, I know that most if not all of those recipients of Canada Works and Young Canada Works funds feel as I do, that it would be better if they could look forward to long-term, career-type jobs which could enable them to plan their lives instead of living from one federal ad hoc job-creation plan to another. How can any young couple possibly plan to set up a home and raise a family when all they can look forward to is a couple of months of work now and again on something like a Canada Works project?
I could say so many things concerning the government's failure to come to grips with unemployment that 1 could use all my allotted time just in talking about that. But I do not want to make the same silly mistake the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) made. If I spoke for the next 24 hours, I would not create a single new job. But the leader of the NDP tries to make us believe that he can create one million new jobs by talking through what would normally be the Easter recess. Obviously, it is not only the government that is mixed up.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Back in March, I think March 22, I asked the chairman of the board of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, William Teron, if he would try to convince the
The Budget-Mr. Darling
government that it would be a good thing to remove the remaining 5 per cent federal sales tax on building materials. Mr. Teron said he would not even consider it. His argument was that the reduction by 6 per cent when the tax had been 11 per cent, had not filtered down to the consumer and he did not believe that removing the remaining 5 per cent would benefit the consumer either. That was a poor argument. Actually it is a cop-out. Mr. Teron was in the building business back in the days when Walter Gordon imposed the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials. I think it was done around 1965. Mr. Teron knows full well what the result of that tax was at that time.
Canada had been experiencing a building boom, and people who had never thought they would be able to afford one were moving into new homes. Mr. Teron knows that the original 11 per cent tax filtered right down to the home buyer. Actually, by the time it got to the buyer the increase was not 11 per cent, but about 17 per cent. He is saying, then, that it is easy to pass along an increase to the consumer, but not possible to pass a decrease along to the consumer. I do not accept that, Mr. Speaker. I doubt very much if Mr. Teron has ever met with the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) to see if either the original 6 per cent cut or a further 5 per cent decrease in tax could be passed on to the consumer.
I can say one thing about it. The consumer will not get the benefit of federal action to bring about such a decrease in taxes unless someone in government is interested enough to ensure that the consumer does get a break.
There is another matter 1 would like to see in the budget and that is an extension of the program whereby the federal government assists homeowners with grants in order to install insulation in their homes to save fuel. This program operates only in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. I do not like my area of Parry Sound-Muskoka being left out of this program. I am not being entirely parochial in this, although I might admit a wee trace of parochialism. The plain fact is that it gets pretty darned cold in my constituency in winter. We pay a higher price for heating oil than some areas further south. There would certainly be some justification for extending this program throughout northern Ontario. Do you hear that, Mr. Nickel Belt?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would be interested in hearing a few words in support of this from some of the more vocal members from northern Ontario as well as from the other northern areas of Canada. I am sure that the mercury sometimes drops in the west as well.
We in the Official Opposition would have liked to have seen some reductions in income tax, and possibly some reductions in federal sales tax. I know you would probably then have the makings of an election budget, but so what? Do we always have to wait until the government feels secure enough to call a
80012-18>/2

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Darling
general election before we can expect tax relief for the lower and middle income wage earners?
The millions of people who are on fixed incomes, those who live on retirement incomes and those on old age security, are the people who would benefit most from a reduction in federal sales tax. However, they are not represented by powerful unions or lobbying groups. They are voiceless, and so they are powerless.
Before I conclude my remarks I would like to refer to my earlier comments on small business and the critical need at this time for legislation that would improve the economic climate in our country for this vital sector of the Canadian economy. I know that the budget proposes several measures that are designed to stimulate interest and support for small business, but the budget does not even begin to face up to this problem. What is needed here is direct, not indirect, assistance to the small business community.
It is interesting to note that at one point in the budget the government proposes direct job creation with massive support for Canada Works and Young Canada Works. Later in the budget we find indirect support in the way of tax credits and deferrals for small businesses, that segment of the economy which accounts for more than 50 per cent of the long-term jobs in this country.
1 do not know how many times I have mentioned in this House that we need a small business administration in Canada that will have no other function or responsibility than to support small businesses in the ways they so badly need support. These areas can be listed as informational, advisory, and financial. This has been done for many years in the United States. If it works somewhere else, why not here?
The small business administration that I envisage would provide up-to-date information on market conditions for a given product or service in the small business sector. It would provide advice on all aspects of starting up a business or improving the operation of an established business. Third, and perhaps most important, it would provide direct access to loan capital to start up a new business or expand an existing business.
I know the government will say there are already programs that will accomplish these things. However, while we have a number of separate and unconnected programs in this area, there are none that provide real assistance to the small businessman or woman. The guaranteed loan program whereby prospective borrowers go to a bank and apply for loans at a couple of percentage points lower than the market rate is unrealistic and unworkable. In the first place most banks do not care as much for the government guarantee as they do for the additional two or three percentage points they would get on a conventional loan. In most cases they would be getting a guarantee from the borrower equal to that offered by the government.
I have heard of cases where an association between a bank and a customer of long standing has been damaged because the customer felt he had a right to the low interest loan. The
[Mr. Darling.)
bank manager felt that he was not entitled to it. Some arguments of bank managers are lame, to put it mildly.
I know of cases where businessmen have been told that their credit was too good, their security was fine and therefore they were not entitled to such a loan. But businessmen who had been customers of banks for a good many years were able to obtain loans at the more attractive rate 20 or 30 miles away. As a result, they transferred their accounts.
While this budget may provide some things, there are certainly many it does not provide. At the present time we have an $11 billion trade deficit. That is frightening. I have been told that a billion dollars of Canadian capital will be going from this country to other countries. It is frightening when our own investors do not have enough confidence in Canada or the present government to invest their money here.
The Canadian taxpayer is paying through the nose. A Canadian family pays 20 per cent of its personal income in taxation. The American equivalent is about 14 per cent. I admit that comparisons are odious. However, when we are constantly shown how much more attractive it is to invest in the United States, we wonder why a great many more people, whether they are students or not, do not take the advice of the Prime Minister when he said that if you do not like it here or cannot find a job here, you can move to another country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mike Landers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the country appears to be suffering from an economic ulcer. Members opposite seem panicky and almost invariably would recommend an immediate operation to cut out the peptic ulcer-and half the stomach with it. However, our Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) did not panic. Essentially what he has done is to put the country on a bland budgetary diet. If this cure does not heal the economic ulcer, I feel confident that my government will know what type of medicine to prescribe in its next budget, which will be an election budget.
During the month of February this year it was my good fortune to be an invited guest of the staff and residents of Fundy Hall, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind facility in Saint John, New Brunswick. During my two hour visit to Fundy Hall, the residents and staff made me aware of some of the problems facing people who are visually handicapped. The notes I have before me today represent the collective experience of a number of visually handicapped people, that is to say, a small group of sightless and partially sighted people made the verbal snowball that is in my hand. On behalf of all visually handicapped Canadians, I will now proceed to throw it.
In relation to employment with the public service, it is a fact that very few visually handicapped people are employed by the Public Service Commission of Canada. Many sightless university graduates complain, and rightfully complain, Mr. Speaker, that they experience great difficulty being seriously considered for employment by the federal government. This
April 5, 1977

complaint is supported by the fact that of over 550,000 federal government employees, only about 50 are registered blind persons. Instead of setting an example for business and industry to follow, the Public Service, the largest employer in Canada, makes little effort to appoint well qualified sightless persons to positions of responsibility. This failure on the part of the Public Service Commission infringes on the rights of the individuals concerned and undermines confidence in the integrity of public officials who have an ethical obligation to make the optimum use of human resources.
Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, this problem will be altered by the passage of the human rights act which prohibits discrimination on the grounds of physical handicap in matters related to employment. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Government of Canada are to be commended for their initiative in this regard. The human rights commission will further alleviate the present imbalance through the use of affirmative action programs.
Partially sighted people complain that when they go to apply for a position with the Public Service Commission the print is so small on the application form as to be obscure even to a person who is not visually handicapped. Surely it would not be an undue imposition on government to make it a requirement that employment application forms be in large, bold type.
In relation to income tax returns, Mr. Speaker, the question was put to me: "Why cannot they be made available in Braille"? The Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) is a kind and thoughtful person and I prod her to examine this worth-while question in an effort to ensure that in 1979, when sightless persons are filling out their tax returns, their fingers will be able to act as their eyes. Surely this particular request meets with all the standards of fairness and reasonableness that average Canadians would normally apply. Although volunteers are usually available to assist sightless people in filing their income tax returns, a number of these individuals would prefer to do it themselves. Nowadays when you are fortunate enough to find someone who wants to do something for himself or herself surely the government should not impede or retard an attitude that is rapidly becoming extinct.
Once the Braille income tax returns become available and are filed, they could be processed by sightless taxation information officers employed by the Department of National Revenue for this purpose. Surely even the opposition members can see the benefits of such an affirmative action program.
In relation to paper currency, Mr. Speaker, on July 8, 1976, I put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this House. I raised a proposal to print paper money with raised bumps on one corner to aid sightless people in readily distinguishing the various denominations. Holland and Switzerland have already taken this initiative. An alternative suggestion is that the Bank of Canada vary the size of the printed note according to value. Many European countries have taken this particular initiative. When this matter was first raised, the Prime Minister seemed incredulous that anyone would cheat a sightless person. The visually handicapped people of Fundy Hall assured me most emphatically that people still prey on
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
and cheat their fellow human beings whose abilities in relation to sight are impaired.
In relation to housing, at present the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation housing program is not flexible enough to meet the needs of sightless people. The co-op housing program is an example; co-op housing developments are usually located in subdivisions far from the centre of town, making accessibility to necessary amenities difficult for the sightless person. Furthermore, a program of this nature requires sweat equity, once again making it infeasible for sightless people to participate.
Generally, very little consideration is given by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to sightless and handicapped people. Rather than making it difficult we should be giving them an incentive to get out of institutions and public housing and to take pride in the accomplishment of achieving home ownership. Perhaps the solution to this is a reduced mortgage over a longer period of time, or a special grant for the sightless and handicapped.
In relation to airlines, Mr. Speaker, the only common complaint is that they do not provide a reduced rate for sightless passengers travelling with escorts. Visually handicapped persons often travel to larger centres for medical attention and require an escort to be with them in the unfamiliar community. It is my submission that sightless people and their escorts should each travel on Air Canada and other airlines at a 50 per cent discount. It is presently CNR's policy to give a 50 per cent discount to a sightless person travelling with an escort.
Althought I raised this particular subject matter in my maiden speech in 1974, the government has not seen fit to embrace the proposal. Well, Mr. Speaker, I shall continue to prod the government in this regard until my proposal is not only embraced but adopted. This particular proposal could be amended to include all physically handicapped people who require escorts when travelling. Having thrown this verbal snowball prepared by the visually handicapped, I implore my government to grab it from mid-air and head for the goal line with it.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have only a few minutes left tonight. However, I suppose that my friends opposite are not unhappy about that. Still I have something to say about the budget which, according to the comments of some ministers and other government members, had led us to entertain some illusions that have been quickly dispelled. We have noted much more disappointment among the Canadian people. It is clear that a few goodies were offered to the taxpayers, taking in consideration the very difficult economic conditions. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) himself said some time ago that the economy was sick. We have known this for a long time and after the efforts he made to bring down his budget in the House, after ten years of efforts on the part of the government, we must unfortunately say that these results have failed miserably.

April 5, 1977
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
These results are due to a complete lack of leadership or insufficient leadership, which of course creates a very unfavourable climate for investment, and therefore a lack of confidence on the part of the population. But the government accuses Canadians of living too high off the hog without realizing, for instance, that 48 per cent of the gross national product is spent by the government itself. We should reflect seriously on this.
The government has made many studies and analyses. It has created various agencies to make recommendations to the cabinet or the government, but this has resulted in the present situation. This places us in a serious difficulty concerning competition with neighbouring countries, with whom we must have trade relationships.
Since trade is increasingly difficult and decreasingly competitive, the government often states that, in view of frozen wages, it is once again the workers who must support the burden of the present situation. I believe we should seriously examine only the income of senior executives. Then we should not have the tendency always to criticize the increases requested by ordinary workers. Even if these increases have been requested, I believe we should consider how the government refused to fight inflation when it was time to do so.
Of course, it now boasts that it has succeeded in partly controlling inflation. I believe that many others than the government or its experts, and especially the Minister of Finance, can claim responsibility for the action taken. I have in front of me the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) who long ago forecast the difficulties that this government would meet. But the government refused to listen to him and tried everything to ridicule him and to make the public believe that his recommendations were senseless.
Today we have come to realize that the government was compelled to do an about turn around, and if it had any success, it did not invent that instrument to partly reduce inflation because the idea came from our former leader on this side of the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh! Not again!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know it does not please my friends opposite if we remind Canadians of the control policy. If the answer suggested by the hon. member for Halifax had been applied, I mean the 90 day freeze period, I think that this government would not have been compelled to deal with problems on a day-to-day basis, according to the circumstances but it did not want to adopt that important part of our program. But eventually it had to apply, for the most part, the program suggested by us. We had proposed an 18 month freeze period and I think we were right. Today, this government, not having obtained the public confidence it needed, does not feel able to start a decontrol process. The minister answers: I want to be sure of cooperation from the provinces, labour, the business community, but I do not think that he will gain their confidence with that kind of budget.
I would like also to encourage this government to undertake a serious selection and analysis of its programs. As I said
(Mr. U Salle.]
earlier, a series of analyses and studies has been made and we know their results, that is the lamentable economic failure of this government. May I invite it to study and reevaluate the services of Statistics Canada?
For example, about the objectives of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion .(Mr. Lessard) aimed at eliminating difficulties stemming from regional inequalities, were those objectives reached? Far from it, and at what cost, Mr. Speaker!
Should the Minister of Finance also be invited to examine the additional costs incurred in the administration of his department? And those astronomical costs also bring results that make us tremble and disappoint us as well. I heard one of my colleagues say during the weekend that if private enterprise had such administrators, considering this budget and its results, that industry would not take long to fire them in view of the poor results they are showing. I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that it is now time to vote.
